item.title: SALES: 9 best affordable hotels in Kyoto
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Kyoto’s hotel scene has moved far beyond the traditional ryokan-versus-business-hotel divide. A wave of boutique openings and international entries has expanded the spectrum in recent years, making it easier than ever for travellers to find stays that balance convenience, style, and affordability. If you're on the hunt for something that won't break the bank, there are plenty of options that range from no-frills hideaways to borderline luxury retreats that deliver remarkable value, all for rates starting at under £265 a night. Timing, however, is everything. The most reasonable rates can be found during winter's quiet months (namely January and February), and again in September's shoulder-season lull. But expect a sharp surge when the cherry blossoms bloom across the city from late March through April, and another more moderate rise during the autumn foliage season in November and early December. Don’t forget to factor in Kyoto’s accommodation tax, too, which is charged per person per night and ranges from ¥200 to ¥1,000 (around 95p to £4.75) depending on the room rate. Whether you’re seeking minimalist modern design, traditional craftsmanship, or sheer value for money, the nine properties below deliver on comfort and character, each with a distinct sense of place. Read on for the best affordable hotels in Kyoto right now. Editor's picks of the best affordable hotels in Kyoto - For Japanese design: Moksa Rebirth Hotel - For unusual interiors: Ace Hotel Kyoto - For a boutique stay: Arashiyama House MAMA How we choose the best affordable hotels in Kyoto Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. This is our pick of the best affordable hotels in Kyoto.

item.title: REVIEW: Enpass Password Manager Review: Private by Design
item.description:
Source: PCMag
Like all password managers, Enpass allows you to create a unique, strong password for every website. Security-wise, you don't have to worry about Enpass suffering from a data breach because the company doesn't keep your private information on its servers. Instead, the app stores your passwords locally or via customer-controlled cloud storage. That's why I like it, despite encountering difficulties when autofilling new credentials during the latest round of testing. That said, if you're looking for a totally free password manager that allows you to create masked emails to prevent spam, Proton Pass is our Editors' Choice. NordPass is our winner for paid password managers because it includes top-notch business and security features at a reasonable price. Previously, you could upload and edit unlimited logins for free using the desktop app. The new free Enpass tier is quite limited, as you can only upload and edit up to 25 logins in your vault. Other free password managers, including Bitwarden, LogMeOnce, and Proton Pass, do not restrict the number of logins you can store in your vault. The Individual Enpass plan costs $23.99 annually and includes unlimited password storage and syncing. You also get security alerts for website breaches, and Enpass will identify accounts in your vault that support multi-factor authentication or passkey creation. A family plan offers the same features for up to six people at $47.99 annually. Alternatively, you can pay a one-time fee of $99.99 to unlock all premium features for a single account, valid for life. Enpass's prices are lower than most of the competition. For example, the Premium tier for 1Password is $35.88, Keeper is $42.99, and LogMeOnce is $30 annually. Bitwarden is the only top app with a lower premium price, at $19.80 per year. Enpass offers apps for Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, and Windows, as well as browser extensions for Brave, Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Opera, Safari, and Vivaldi. Enpass used to offer a portable version of the password manager that you could load onto a thumb drive and use without installing it directly on a computer or mobile device, but that feature has been discontinued. To start using Enpass, download and install the app, then provide and confirm your email address. Next, create a master password to encrypt all your data. This password should be memorable but not guessable by anyone else. Enpass rates your master password and offers specific advice for improving a bad one—noting, for example, that what you've typed contains a name or a common password. Your master password is irretrievable, so be sure to write it down in a secure location. Enpass handles credential storage differently than many password managers. After you log in to the app, Enpass allows you to choose where to store your vault data. You have two options: Store your passwords locally on your device or keep them in a third-party cloud storage account. This means that if you want to use the password manager app on multiple devices, you will need to sync your credentials using a third-party cloud service, such as Google Drive, or a shared Wi-Fi connection. To store your credentials using your own cloud storage, go to Settings > Vaults in the desktop app, select the vault you want to sync, and choose Set Up Sync. Then you need to give Enpass permission to create a folder in your Box, Dropbox, Google Drive, iCloud, or OneDrive account. You can also use a shared network folder. I had no trouble setting up storage and syncing credentials across devices using a third-party cloud account. However, I encountered some setbacks when attempting to sync credentials stored locally from one device to another. The server and your target devices must be connected to the same Wi-Fi network for the feature to work. The benefit of this setup is that your data never leaves your home network. I was unable to fully test this feature because the desktop computer I use for testing lacks Wi-Fi connectivity. Syncing is more straightforward with most other password managers because the data is stored on the company's cloud-based servers. However, these servers are juicy targets for hackers, so storing your data locally whenever possible is safer. Enpass imports credential lists from many competitors, including Bitwarden, Dashlane, and RoboForm. If your old password manager isn't on the list, never fear. Export your list from your old app to a CSV file and import it to your Enpass vault. Enpass doesn’t offer the typical multi-factor authentication (MFA) options for its apps, such as codes generated by authenticator apps or authentication via hardware security keys. According to an Enpass spokesperson, the reason is as follows: "Enpass users store their vaults in spaces they control, [and] there are already multiple extra layers of authentication between those vaults and anyone trying to access them." Enpass doesn't store customer data on its servers, so I don't think requiring MFA for its apps is necessary. Enpass's lack of MFA does not affect the product's score. I recommend ensuring that your phone and computer unlock with biometrics, such as a face or fingerprint scan, or a passcode. That way, if you lose your device or someone steals it, your private data is a little harder to extract. Before reviewing and testing a password manager, I send the company questions about its privacy and security practices. I do this to hold companies accountable for safeguarding your private data. The answers below provide information about Enpass's privacy and security policies, allowing you to make an informed decision before downloading a new app or browser extension. Has your company ever had a security breach? No. What unencrypted information does the password manager store in user vaults? None — everything is encrypted. What is the company's policy regarding selling or sharing customer data with third parties? No user data is sold or shared. How does your company respond to requests for user information from governments and law enforcement? Enpass has no access to any data users store in their Enpass vaults. We call this "Zero Possession" to help distinguish how Enpass works from the "zero knowledge" claims of password managers that actually do have access to their users' data. If required by subpoena, law, or other legal process, in some circumstances Enpass may provide a user's name and email, but this is the only personal information Enpass has about any user. Enpass's answers align with the company's privacy policy. I encourage anyone in the market for a new password manager to browse each app's privacy policies to learn more about how companies collect, sell, or store user data. You can open Enpass mobile apps using biometrics, such as a fingerprint or face scan. In the app's Settings menu, you can configure app timeouts and unlock methods. While you're there, check out some of the security tweaks I recommend below. First, I suggest enabling the Hide Sensitive option in the Security settings menu. It will obscure your password fields to protect you from over-the-shoulder snoops. Next, go to the Advanced section of the Settings menu. There, you'll find the option to scan your vault for passwords exposed in a data breach. In a post on the support site, Enpass explains that scans occur locally on your device and That It doesn't send your passwords to a third party, which is ideal. Below that setting is the Erase Everything option. It nukes your vault, keeping your passwords safe and secure in the cloud or on another device. Vault data stored via third-party cloud storage, on a USB drive, or on other devices will not be affected. It's helpful if you think your device has been compromised and want to keep your data out of the wrong hands. I like Enpass' vault audit functions, which identify breached, compromised, identical, MFA-protected, passkey-supported, or weak logins in your vault. Other password managers, like RoboForm, offer similar password hygiene tools. I was impressed with the Security Score feature, which rates your password health. Most other password managers still give users an inflated score, even with compromised or weak passwords, but Enpass is a lot more strict. I keep weak and compromised logins in my test vaults to measure the efficacy of password managers' hygiene tools, and my ultra-low score (35) is appropriate. For this review, I tested Enpass on an iPhone, as well as the Chrome and Firefox browser extensions and the Windows app. The desktop app is easy to navigate, and it's required to use the browser extensions. I didn't have trouble capturing and storing existing logins in my vault, but I ran into a little trouble when trying to create a new Reddit account using both the Chrome and Firefox browser extensions. Enpass failed to capture the new credentials, so I had to manually copy and paste them into a new entry in my vault. If you use the browser extension, check the box that requires Enpass to authenticate all your new sessions. This is one way to prevent someone from using your browser's old authenticated session tokens to steal your credentials. I successfully created and stored passkeys using Enpass. You can manage your passkeys by clicking or tapping on the Passkeys section in your vault. From there, you can edit the entry to include other info, such as an associated phone number, a security question, or a secret key for a one-time code. I always tell people to create long, strong, and unique passwords for their accounts, and Enpass makes that task easy. The password generator creates a 32-character password by default, which is excellent. The maximum is 100 characters. Your passwords can include capital and lowercase letters, digits, and symbols. Beyond Passwords: IDs, Forms, and Attachments In addition to passkeys and passwords, you can store various types of information in your Enpass vault, including addresses, phone numbers, and even your Social Security number. That said, I don't recommend storing all your private information in a single app, even if it's stored locally. If someone accesses your device, they'll have all of that information. Instead, consider keeping your private data and files on a storage device that isn't connected to the internet, like a thumb drive or a portable hard drive. Enpass can auto-fill details such as your name, address, or phone number on the web, making quick work of shopping checkout forms or information requests on government websites. During the latest evaluation, Enpass recognized the form field and offered to fill in the name or email address I stored in my vault. I like that you can create multiple identities in Enpass, so you can have one for social media, another for gaming, and another for shopping. You can attach files and images to your vault entries. For example, you could add a photo of your driver's license to the corresponding item. Your storage space is limited to the amount left on your local device or in the cloud storage account you set up. Sharing Is Clunky, and There's No Emergency Access I don't normally advise sharing passwords, but there are relatively low-risk situations where sharing makes sense. To share a vault credential with another person who uses Enpass, first create a pre-shared key (PSK) for the credential you want to share. The PSK is a password you create and send to the recipient or group before sending the password itself. The shared passwords are only accessible via the Enpass app. Other password managers make sharing a little easier and more intuitive. For example, Keeper allows you to designate different levels of security for your shared passwords. You can also create separate vaults for sharing passwords with family and friends, which is handy if you share a Netflix account with family members or need access to a fantasy football account with friends. Enpass does not currently offer any password inheritance or other emergency access features, which would facilitate the transfer of your credentials and other valuable information in the event of your untimely demise. Bitwarden, Dashlane, Keeper, and NordPass all offer digital inheritance methods. Mobile: A Capable Companion, Not a Replacement I tested the Enpass iOS app. The app's appearance is comparable to the browser extension and desktop version, but it's not quite as functional. For example, there's no way to upload your password list from your phone. You can still access any vaults you’ve synced, manage tags, use all the password audit tools, and generate passwords. The Enpass mobile app can also serve as an authenticator, allowing you to scan QR codes and generate MFA tokens. I was able to use my synced passwords on my mobile device and log in to my test accounts without any problems. If you have trouble auto-filling your logins, visit your device's Settings menu to ensure that Enpass is set as your default password manager. Support, Cancellation, and Account Deletion Need help with your Enpass account? You can email [email protected] for assistance. If you'd like to try troubleshooting the problem on your own, visit the Enpass support website or ask a question in the app's forums. If you ever want to move on from Enpass and switch to a new password manager, you must cancel your subscription before you can fully delete your account. If you subscribed to the app through Apple's App Store or Google Play Store, you'll need to cancel the subscription in those apps. If you bought your subscription on Enpass' website, visit this link, enter your email address, and then follow the link you receive in your email inbox to access your account page, where you can cancel your subscription. After canceling your subscription, deleting your account is a very straightforward process, which is ideal. Open the Settings menu on any platform, tap your email address, then select Delete Account. Enpass used to offer three levels of service for businesses, but the company has since trimmed those down to just one offering, the Business Plan, which costs $1.99 per user per month. There's also an Enterprise Plan for larger companies. Like the personal plan, the Business plan lets users store data locally on their devices and use cloud storage. Key highlights of the plan include access recovery, vault sharing, complimentary family plans for all employees, custom branding options, and automatic user provisioning via SCIM from trusted platforms like Azure AD and Okta. All business accounts include integration with Google Workspace and Microsoft 365. As with competitors NordPass and Dashlane, Enpass Business features an audit system for users and a security dashboard for administrators. The reporting dashboard shows which employees have weak, reused, or old passwords in their vaults. One helpful feature of Enpass Business is automatic offboarding. It enables administrators to automatically delete data from employee devices and vaults when employees leave the organization. Competitor Bitwarden has a similar function: admin users can remove team members from vaults at their discretion. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Enpass is a capable, affordable password manager built around a rare strength: You decide where your vault lives, and the company never holds your data. Its strict security audits, passkey support, and excellent password generator impress, and premium plans cost less than most rivals. But inconsistent autofill, failed captures of new logins, clunky sharing, no emergency access, and a free tier capped at 25 logins hold it back. If you want a free password manager, Proton Pass remains our Editors' Choice for its ease of use and perks like masked email addresses. If you're willing to pay, NordPass is our pick for premium password management, with top-notch security and business features at a reasonable price. STILL ON THE FENCE? - ● The Best Business Password Managers for 2026 - ● The Best Password Managers for Google Chrome I review privacy tools like hardware security keys, password managers, private messaging apps, and ad-blocking software. I also report on online scams and offer advice to families and individuals about staying safe on the internet. Before joining PCMag, I wrote about tech and video games for CNN, Fanbyte, Mashable, The New York Times, and TechRadar. I also worked at CNN International, where I did field producing and reporting on sports that are popular with worldwide audiences. In addition to the categories below, I exclusively cover ad blockers, authenticator apps, hardware security keys, and private messaging apps.

item.title: SALES: The 20 best places to travel in 2027
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
These 20 destinations chosen by BBC editors offer extraordinary experiences, new reasons to visit and different ways of seeing the world in 2027. You don't need us to sell you on New York or Venice. But did you know that one of the world's most remote islands is now inviting adventurous travellers to discover its shores? Or that in 2027, travellers to Japan can witness an ancient ritual that takes place just once in a generation? For our guide to the best places to travel in 2027, we're looking beyond the perennial favourites to destinations offering something remarkable in the year ahead. Each offers unforgettable experiences – and opportunities to make a positive difference to the people and environments that make them special. Why go: Experience unique, endangered wildlife while helping to protect it With 92% of its mammals found nowhere else on Earth, Madagascar offers extraordinary wildlife encounters. The panther chameleon and the "dancing" Verreaux's sifaka are among the unique species inhabiting its rainforests, sandstone canyons and otherworldly landscapes. And with the country seeking to increase visitation three-fold in the next two years, travelling responsibly can help protect its remaining wild spaces and nearly 10,000 endemic plants and animals. In 2027, Mitsinjo Reserve's much-anticipated 150-hectare reforestation corridor will plant its final trees, restoring habitat for lemurs, fossas and reptiles. Elsewhere, the Anja Community Reserve uses park fees to fund healthcare and education initiatives. "It holds the highest concentration of ring-tailed lemurs in the world – and they're really easy to spot in the reserve," says Sarah Faith from Responsible Travel. Stay at the Anja Reserve Lodge to enjoy their luxury suites and meals featuring local products against the dramatic backdrop of the Three Sisters massif. In western Madagascar, sample French-Malagasy cuisine at Le Mad Zebu en route to the limestone spires of Tsingy de Bemaraha, part of a Unesco World Heritage site. – Geena Truman Signature experience: Ranomafana, the granite massifs of Anja and the sunny southern coast. Abundant wildlife sightings are nearly guaranteed. Why go: Explore the first entire city in the world to be designated a Unesco Biosphere Reserve The cobblestoned capital of French-speaking Canada sits where the St Lawrence River widens seaward, with Laurentian summits rolling north beyond the city limits. Quebec City's Old World charm may draw first-time visitors, but its setting encourages them to explore beyond the historic streets – whether cross-country skiing across the Plains of Abraham, a 103-hectare park and 18th-Century battlefield, or discovering its buzzy new waterfront. Accessible outdoors and sustainability strides recently made Quebec City the world's first city whose entirety is designated a Unesco Biosphere Reserve. Waterfront revitalisations are luring bathers to the L'Oasis du Port de Quebec, North America's first urban harbour swimming facility; while a floating sauna complex debuting there in December 2026 will offer cold plungers a sleek way to warm up. The city's history, meanwhile, extends beyond colonial-era landmarks. At the nearby Indigenous Huron-Wendat community of Wendake, travellers can encounter ancestral stories while strolling Onhwa' Lumina, a 1.2km (0.75 miles) forest pathway lined with video projections. – Jen Rose Smith Signature experience: Take an ice-canoeing class in Quebec City (December to March). The quintessentially Quebecois sport features teams alternately paddling and sprinting across the partially frozen St Lawrence River. Why go: Witness an ancient, once-in-a-generation ritual in Japan's Shinto heartland Far from the "golden route" of Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka, Ise Shima Peninsula offers immersion into a rural Japanese seafaring community steeped in 2,000 years of Shinto spirituality. This jagged coastline is home to natural bays, deep forests and Ise Jingu, the nation's most sacred Shinto shrine. In summer 2027, visitors have a rare chance to experience the ancient tradition of okihiki. The 1,300-year-old summer ritual happens every 20 years when locals haul enormous cypress logs to rebuild the city's shrines by hand (in 2027, weekends from 8 May-12 June; 24 July-1 August). Snag a prime viewing spot along the Isuzu River to enjoy the festive buzz and watch thousands of chanting participants in white happi coats march through the streets of Ise City in a celebration of sustainability and craftsmanship. Pay respects at Ise Jingu shrine, or explore Ise Shima National Park, where you can also tour Mikimoto Pearl Island – the birthplace of Japan's modern cultured-pearl industry. – Michelle Gross Signature experience: Visit Osatsu Ama Hut Why go: Visit one of the world's most remote islands as it cautiously opens to more travellers Located in the South Atlantic, midway between Africa and South America, this 122-sq-km (47sq-mile) island remains strikingly undeveloped, with no international hotel chains or global fast-food brands. Until 2017, almost every visitor arrived by sea. Today, St Helena is opening up to tourism slowly and on its own terms. A 98-seat weekly flight connects the island with Johannesburg, bringing adventurous travellers to its volcanic landscapes, close-knit communities and Napoleonic history. Its capital, Jamestown, is unlike anywhere else in the world, with Georgian buildings squeezed into a dramatic volcanic valley that opens onto the ocean. In 2027, St Helena Adventure Week will draw travellers for hiking, kayaking and open-water swimming, culminating in the inaugural World's Most Remote Marathon on 28 February. For St Helena, though, attracting visitors is about survival. With a population of around 4,000 and many younger Saints leaving for work, tourism is being developed to support local livelihoods while protecting the island's fragile landscapes and communities. – Ellie Cobb Signature experience: Climb Jamestown's 699-step Jacob's Ladder, rising almost vertically from the capital for sweeping views across the volcanic valley and South Atlantic. Why go: Salvador steps onto the world stage for the 2027 Fifa Women's World Cup Wedged between the emerald waters of the Bay of All Saints and the Atlantic Ocean, Salvador instantly wins visitors over with its warm welcome and sea views. But its rich culture rewards a closer look: once a hub of the brutal transatlantic slave trade, Brazil's first capital is steeped in the traditions and religions of the African diáspora, from the hypnotic sway of capoeira to the vats of hot oil filled with sizzling acarajé – an iconic street food that originates in religious candomblé rituals. Salvador will be in the global spotlight in 2027 as a host city for the Fifa Women's World Cup – the first edition ever held in South America. Beyond the stadium, visitors can explore its rich Afro-Brazilian heritage in Unesco-listed Pelourinho, with its cobbled streets, weathered colonial houses and Baroque churches, and at MUNCAB, home to one of the country's finest collections of Afro-Brazilian art. – Catherine Balston Signature experience: Take a boat across the Bay of All Saints to Ilha dos Frades, a tiny pedestrian-only island of forested hills and crystal-clear waters. Climb 130 steps to the 17th-Century chapel of Nossa Senhora de Guadalupe for sweeping bay views, then cool off with a swim and a Bahian seafood lunch on the beach. Why go: A landmark protection status offers a new reason to experience this timeless, otherworldly landscape Paddling into the Okefenokee, North America's largest blackwater swamp, is like travelling through time. This 684-sq-mile (1,771-sq-km) primordial paradise has scarcely changed in 6,500 years. Straddling the Georgia-Florida line, its 120 miles (193km) of water trails weave through moss-draped cypress stands, sawtooth palmetto-covered islands and lily-dappled channels dyed black by peat deposits. Here, alligators congregate by the hundreds and pterodactyl-like wood storks roost. In 2026, Unesco named part of the swamp a World Heritage site – the US's first natural site inscribed in more than 30 years, fortifying its protection against mining proposals that risked draining this fragile ecosystem. Newcomers can get to know it on a naturalist-guided tour, or make their own way: raised boardwalks invite birders and outdoors-lovers to hop out of a canoe, kayak or small motorboat (available for rent) and explore on foot. – Alexandra Marvar Signature experience: Secure a wilderness camping permit and paddle to an over-water camping platform in Okefenokee State Park on a night with a new Moon, where you can stargaze in this gold-tier Dark Sky-certified wilderness to a soundtrack of frog song. Why go: France is marking the bicentenary of photography until September 2027, with the story rooted around Chalon-sur-Saône Home to celebrated vineyards, honey-stone villages and the world's most famous mustard, Burgundy hardly needs a new reason to visit. But in 2027, one of France's most classic regions has a fresh way to be seen: as the birthplace of photography. Start at Chalon-sur-Saône's Musée Nicéphore Niépce, where the world's oldest surviving camera photograph will return for a special exhibition from late April to late June 2027, before continuing to nearby Saint-Loup-de-Varennes, where Niépce created that very image 200 years ago. Explore Dijon's medieval streets and bustling market halls, then follow the 60km (37-mile) Route des Grands Crus south through the Unesco-listed vineyard landscapes of the Côte d'Or to Beaune and Volnay, host of the famous Saint-Vincent Tournante wine festival (30-31 January 2027). Along the way are Romanesque churches, village bistros and family-run producers whose work keeps local food and wine traditions alive. Be sure to end the day with a glass of Burgundy in one of the region's centuries-old villages. – Ellie Cobb Signature experience: Visit La Moutarderie Fallot in Beaune, Burgundy's historic mustard mill, to discover the history and production of the region's iconic condiment. Finish with a tasting at the mustard bar. Why go: Discover living root bridges, sacred forests and mountain communities from a local homestay The north-eastern Indian state of Meghalaya is home to centuries-old living root bridges that span deep gorges and rivers across the lush Khasi and Jaintia hills, where Indigenous communities have lived in harmony with the landscape for generations. But in 2027, it is also set to become one of India's most exciting destinations for community-based travel. Ahead of the 39th National Games in March 2027, Meghalaya is supporting the creation or upgrading of 1,000 homestays, allowing visitors to experience the state's natural and cultural heritage while ensuring tourism benefits local communities. "Travellers can join guided nature walks, learn about traditional weaving and handicrafts, and experience food tourism rooted in foraging traditions and local agricultural products such as Lakadong turmeric," says Kaitlyn Brajcich from Sustainable Travel International. To explore the region, visitors can trek through the Unesco-recognised Nokrek Biosphere Reserve, visit Mawphlang's sacred groves and see Shillong in full bloom during November's Cherry Blossom Festival. Along the way, relish a mountain cuisine rich in foraged ingredients, experience Meghalaya's celebrated rock music scene and meet the artisans keeping the 1,000-year-old Lyrnai black pottery craft alive. – Soumya Gayatri Signature experience: Hike to Nongriat's extraordinary double-decker living root bridge, where generations of Khasi people have trained the aerial roots of rubber fig trees into resilient pathways through one of the world's wettest landscapes. Why go: Celebrate 70 years of independence in a nation that helped shape Africa When Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African nation to gain independence from European colonial rule in 1957, it inspired liberation movements across the continent. Seventy years later, the anniversary coincides with Beyond the Return, the country's long-term initiative encouraging the African diaspora to reconnect through heritage, culture and exchange – while giving all travellers a timely reason to explore Ghana's complex past and creative present. Start on the coast at the Unesco-listed castles of Cape Coast and Elmina, where Panafest, Ghana's biennial pan-African arts and culture festival, returns in 2027, with ceremonies and performances reflecting on the legacy of the transatlantic slave trade. Then head to Accra for contemporary galleries and fashion studios, Afrobeats music and an inventive dining scene. Further east on the Volta coast, the Meet Me There Eco Lodge offers low-key lodging beside a saltwater lagoon, with every stay funding sanitation and education projects in two neighbouring villages. "For visitors, it's magical," says Responsible Travel's co-founder, Justin Francis. "Travellers get everything a luxury beach holiday should be, but they also get an authentic insight into rural Ghanian village life." – Ellie Cobb Signature experience: Walk Kakum National Park's canopy walkway, where seven suspension bridges carry visitors high above the tropical rainforest. Why go: New openings in the world's oldest tropical rainforest Where the world's oldest tropical rainforest meets the Great Barrier Reef, the Daintree packs ancient forest, white-sand beaches and extraordinary wildlife – from prehistoric-looking cassowaries to elusive tree kangaroos – into one of Australia's most dramatic landscapes. In 2027, new Indigenous-led experiences are giving travellers deeper insights into the culture that has shaped this place for tens of thousands of years. At Kulki/Cape Tribulation, a new Aboriginal-owned visitor hub introduces travellers to Eastern Kuku Yalanji stories through interpretive exhibits and artworks. Other guided experiences take you further into Kuku Yalanji Country, combining rainforest walks with storytelling, ceremony and access to sacred cultural sites. Kaitlyn Brajcich from Sustainable Travel International suggests travellers taste their way through the region on the Daintree Food Trail, winding between rainforest-clad mountains and Coral Sea beaches to small farms and producers serving everything from tropical fruit and gelato to barramundi and chocolate. "Several use Wet Tropics native ingredients that carry deep significance in Kuku Yalanji ecological knowledge" she says. Scheduled to open in December 2026, the ultra-luxury Ever Bloomfield eco-lodge will offer an exclusive new base for exploring the rainforest and reef. – Sarah Reid Signature experience: Join a First Nations-guided Dreamtime Walk at Mossman Gorge Centre, beginning with a traditional smoking ceremony before exploring culturally significant sites and learning about bush foods, animal significance and traditional plant use. Why go: A new cycling path takes explorers to peaks, canyons, lakes and Slovenia's unique model of sustainability Spread across a mountain-framed valley in north-western Slovenia's Julian Alps, the municipality of Bohinj consists of 24 villages surrounding its eponymous glacial lake. A new cycling link completed in mid-2026 connects Bled and Lake Bohinj along a 28km (17.4-mile) route, inviting travellers to explore this stunning, yet often overlooked region. Follow the edge of Triglav National Park along the Sava Bohinjka River to pedal past forests, waterfalls, 17th-Century churches and Iron Age settlements. "[The trail] allows visitors to cycle safely through alpine landscapes between two of Slovenia's most iconic lakes for the first time," says Kaitlyn Brajcich from Sustainable Travel International. The route is just one recent example of how Bohinj is using tourism to protect fragile landscapes. Stop at Camp Danica to try locally certified sausages and cheeses, and stay in one of their five new eco-conscious wooden "glamping" cabins, inaugurated in 2026, to experience Bohinj's sustainability model in style. – Alex Crevar Signature experience: Hike into Triglav National Park's spectacular Seven Lakes Valley where a chain of glacial lakes lies beneath the towering peaks of the Julian Alps. Why go: See the space race come to a remote Scottish isle The Shetland island of Unst boasts the northernmost everything in Britain, while also being one of Europe's most history-laden small islands. Its remarkable Viking heritage includes the remains of more than 60 longhouses – the highest density of rural Viking sites anywhere, including Scandinavia. But in 2027, Unst will be spotlighting a very different kind of voyaging: space rockets. Remote Unst has been chosen as the home of SaxaVord, the UK's first licensed spaceport for vertical rocket launches, where maiden orbital lift-offs are being planned for 2027. Apply for one of around 600 passes for the launch pad viewing site – or just camp out at the golden sands of Burrafirth Beach, where you can scan for whales as well as watch rockets soar spaceward. Between blastoffs, roam Muness Castle, Britain's most northerly fortification, or browse Unst's atmospheric artisanal museums, before raising a glass at the UK's most northerly pub, the Balta Light, with local brews and Shetland food plus local bands. – Norman Miller Signature experience: Delve into Unst's maritime heritage at the Unst Boat Haven, where traditional Shetland vessels include the Far Haaf, a six-oared open boat once used by brave deep-sea fishermen. Why go: Venture beyond Korea's bustling cities to explore its mountainous, spiritual heartland With flashy Seoul welcoming record numbers of international visitors, mountainous Gangwon province offers pristine landscapes and a glimpse into another side of South Korea, where Buddhist temples, mountain spirits and shamanic traditions remain woven into rural life. Take an intercity train to Chuncheon, Gangwon's scenic lakeside capital, for its signature dak galbi (spicy chicken stir-fry), then hop on a bus to the Inner Seorak, the secluded interior of Seoraksan National Park. Here, hikers can explore mist-shrouded trails winding through deep valleys, passing waterfalls, serene Buddhist temples and hermitages. Head east to the coastal city of Sokcho for jogae-gui (fresh shellfish grilled over coals) then continue south to seaside Gangneung, where each June, evenings come alive with the shamanic rituals, mask dances and the hypnotic music of the ancient Gangneung Danoje Festival. – Ben McKechnie Signature experience: Join the Nimui Chimmuk (The Silence of the Beloved) temple-stay programme at historic Baekdamsa Temple, where meditation, mountain walks through tranquil Okryu Valley and Buddhist ceremonies invite participants to slow down and reconnect with nature. Why go: A new chapter for a beloved national park and an immersion in Indigenous history Few places in Canada have a stronger sense of identity than Alberta – something brought into sharp focus by the province's recent separatist debates. In 2027, the 150th anniversary of Treaty 7, a historic agreement between the Crown and the region's First Nations, offers an opportunity to explore a much longer history of sovereignty and belonging. Events at its signing site, Blackfoot Crossing, and The Confluence in Calgary invite visitors to learn about the Indigenous histories of region that long predate it. Calgary is also celebrating the reopening of the Glenbow Museum in autumn 2027 with new galleries highlighting Blackfoot history and contemporary Indigenous art. Visitors can explore it and the new major sports and entertainment venue, Scotia Place (which is inspired by Indigenous culture and Alberta's landscapes) via the city's recently expanded 1,000km pathway system. To the west, Jasper National Park is reemerging after the devastating 2024 wildfire. Linking bright blue glacial lakes, the Valley of the Five Lakes Trail is reopening in 2027, while the new Pleckaitis Canyon Icewalk leads visitors into one of Jasper's deepest accessible canyons. The beloved Tekarra Lodge, The Robson and Maligne Lodge – now Jasper's first boutique wellness hotel, complete with a hydrothermal sauna – are each reopening in summer 2027. – Diane Selkirk Signature experience: Join Jasper's Warrior Women for an Indigenous cultural experience, learning about local plants, culture and art and gathering around the fire for stories, drumming and singing. Why go: With nearly two sheep per person, Sardinia is Italy without the crowds The Mediterranean's second-largest island has long been known as a seaside escape. But beyond its glitzy Costa Smeralda resorts, Sardinia's seldom-explored interior shelters one of Italy's last unspoilt corners. Here, craggy massifs and twisting valleys reveal a Tolkien-esque world dotted with 800 "giants' tombs", 3,500 newly Unesco-inscribed "fairy houses" and 7,000 stone towers from one of the world's most mysterious Bronze Age civilisations. The launch of the first two direct flights from the US to Sardinia in 2026 and 2027 brings the island within easier reach – just as the island is encouraging visitors to venture beyond its famous coast. The Santa Barbara Mining Route, recently voted the world's best slow-travel trail by Komoot users, immerses travellers in one of Sardinia's least-explored corners. Meanwhile, the island is investing €38m (£31.8m/$42m) in rural communities to develop tourism while preserving sarditá (Sardinian identity), celebrated each autumn during the Autunno in Barbagia festival. – Eliot Stein Signature experience: Stay at Su Gologone, Why go: A remarkable urban revival and a newly recognised food scene Long seen mainly as a gateway to New Zealand's South Island, Christchurch has reinvented itself more than 15 years after the earthquakes that devastated the city. The revitalised Ōtākaro Avon River Precinct, an expanded network of walking and cycling routes and major new venues such as the One New Zealand stadium are giving travellers more reason to stay in the city itself. Ngāi Tahu, the local Māori people, have helped shape the rebuild, with their stories and cultural values woven into the urban design. Michelin's arrival in New Zealand has also put Christchurch's food scene firmly in the spotlight, with two Michelin-starred restaurants, 10 Bib Gourmands and chefs making the most of Canterbury-grown produce, Banks Peninsula seafood and wines from nearby North Canterbury. New seasonal Air New Zealand flights from Singapore, Tokyo and Perth are improving access, while surf beaches, vineyards and the Southern Alps are all within easy reach. – Ellie Cobb Signature experience: Paddle a traditional Māori waka (canoe) along the Ōtākaro Avon River with local guides, learning how the river has long served as source of food, culture and connection – and how it is being restored today. Why go: A lesser-known corner of Transylvania becomes a European Region of Gastronomy Thanks partly to a certain literary vampire, Transylvania – the land "beyond the forest" – hovers somewhere between fact and fiction. In reality, this bucolic region in central Romania is a mosaic of villages wreathed in bear-rich woodlands and cloaked in a meditative serenity. In eastern Transylvania, Harghita County is the heartland of the Székely, a Hungarian-speaking community whose culinary traditions are rooted in smoking, pickling, baking, foraging, cheese-making and preserving for long winters. Haymaking is still done with scythes. In 2027, this little-known corner of Transylvania becomes a European Region of Gastronomy, giving travellers a reason to look beyond the Dracula clichés and into its kitchens, farms and village pensiuni (guesthouses). A new Signature Dish programme will showcase 50 representative local dishes, from potato bread and mountain cheeses to forest mushrooms and berry preserves. – Andrew Eames Signature experience: For a true taste of Harghita, ask your local pensiune (guesthouse) to arrange dinner: think potato soup, roast pork, sheep's cheese and zacuscă, a paste made from roasted red peppers. And perhaps a carafe of village-distilled pálinka brandy, strong enough to blow your socks off. Why go: World-class hikes, sky-high views and ancient civilisations A crinkled mass of ice-capped peaks jutting 400km (250 miles) north-east of Lima, the Cordillera Blanca is a region of brilliant turquoise lakes, traditional Andean villages and hiking trails forged by ancient civilisations. Here, more than 500 glaciers and dozens of mountain-passes topping 4,500m (14,763ft) make the Alps look like miniatures. The area's trails are anchored by the four-day Santa Cruz Trek – the so-called "Inca Trail of the North" – and dotted with ruins, including the citadel of Chavín de Huántar, the remnant of a sophisticated society that flourished long before the rise of the Inca Empire. In a governmental bid to promote the nation's less-visited regions, new flights have recently been introduced between Lima and the hub city of Huaraz. Other developments include the asphalting of a spectacular east-west highway across the Cordillera, recent improvements of the region's most iconic day-hike to Laguna 69 and the long-awaited opening of Huaraz's new Neoclassical cathedral 57 years after the original was destroyed in an earthquake. – Brendan Sainsbury Signature experience: Hike the 14km (8.7-mile) high-altitude trail to Laguna 69 surrounded by river meadows, tumbling waterfalls and unobstructed views of some of South America's highest mountains. Why go: A thriving art scene in a spectacular, snowcapped setting Located in the foothills of the snowcapped Tian Shan mountains and overshadowed by the Silk Road cities of Bukhara and Samarkand, Almaty typically flies under travellers' radars. But the culinary, art and design scene of this cosmopolitan Kazakh city at the crossroads of Europe and Asia is increasingly attracting international attention. In 2027, new nonstop flights are expected to connect Almaty to New York, Abu Dhabi and Hong Kong. Central Asia's first major contemporary art museum, the Almaty Museum of Art and the Asif Khan-designed Tselinny Center of Contemporary Culture opened here late last year. Both showcase the region's nomad identity rooted in Tengri, a world view pre-dating Islam that reveres the steppe and natural world. Elsewhere, Almaty-based artisans are reimagining Kazakh craftsmanship at galleries throughout the city, and next summer, The Spirit of Tengri music festival will showcase hundreds of global, regional and Kazakh artists on open-air stages across the city. – Yulia Denisyuk Why go: Experience the modern revival of an ancient Japanese hot spring town Six hundred years ago, a Shinto deity allegedly bequeathed a thermal spring to the monks of Tainei-ji temple in westernmost Yamaguchi, giving rise to the resort town of Nagato Yumoto. Today, thanks to a revamp of the hot spring and a decade-long, community-led restoration, it's drawing visitors to one of Japan's least-visited prefectures. In 2027, the town marks 600 years since the spring's legendary discovery. The anniversary is being celebrated with a Kento-shiki (hot spring dedication ceremony) on 4 January at the atmospheric Tainei-ji Temple. From 15 January to 7 March, admire the annual Otozuregawa Utaakari nighttime illuminations around Otozure River Park; year-round, stay at the design-forward Soil Hotel, which offers e-biking to nearby sea crags, historic soy sauce breweries and the hillside kilns used 350 years ago to fire Hagi-yaki pottery, still crafted here today. Refuel with Yamaguchi-style kawara soba cooked on a black roof tile at the rustic Yanagiya restaurant. – Paul Bloomfield Signature experience: Bathe at the renovated, historic hot spring, restored and reopened as the industrial-chic Onto Onsen. Soaking in the alkaline-rich waters has been long-believed to restore body and soul. BBC Travel editors, trusted journalists and sustainable tourism experts from around the world nominated destinations with a compelling reason to visit in 2027. We looked particularly for places using tourism to benefit local communities, protect the environment, preserve cultural heritage and encourage more thoughtful ways to travel. The 20 destinations are presented in no particular order. – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: REVIEW: It shouldn’t be this easy to pedal 25 mph: Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica
I’ve had only one experience of pedaling an e-bike after it ran out of juice, but it was enough to make checking the battery display an anxiety-driven habit: “Can I afford to use the highest assist level up this hill? Should I switch to eco mode to preserve power and make sure I have enough to get home with the bike lights on?” These aren’t fun questions to have rattling around in your head while riding home in the dark. But those intrusive thoughts never crossed my mind while I was testing Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo. I didn’t experience range anxiety, even while blowing through city streets at 25-plus mph (40.2 kph). The bike has so much juice (840 watt-hours) and power (810 watts of peak power and 105 newton-meters of torque) from Specialized’s 3.1 motor system that I could ride as far and as fast as I wanted without worrying about having enough battery to get back home. Given my preference for biking over driving, I need a bike that can get me across town at a decent clip without draining an entire charge. That’s exactly what the Evo delivered on my longest rides. What sold me on the bike was a 24-mile round trip that took 83 minutes and used just 56 percent of the battery. According to Specialized’s app, which connects to the bike over Bluetooth, I averaged 235 W of assist power while moving an average of 17 mph, though I was generally closer to 20 mph on stretches where I didn’t have to slow down. I also hit a max speed of 27.3 mph with little effort. The bike is a beast, weighing around 70 pounds for the large-size frame I tested. Despite being the heaviest e-bike I’ve ridden, the Evo makes pedaling easier than ever. The bike lacks a throttle, so it takes a few rotations to get moving, but once the assist kicks in, it’s remarkable how easily you can reach the 18–20 mph range.

item.title: SALES: Best Video Editing Software for Beginners
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
Best Video Editing Software for Beginners Some of the more expensive editors can make your first few videos unnecessarily complicated, that’s why you don’t really need professional editing software to start a YouTube channel or put together a decent travel vlog. When comparing the best video editing software for beginners, we looked at how easy it is to assemble footage, what each editor can automate, and how much room there is to experiment with different editing techniques. We also considered what you can actually export without paying because a free download doesn’t always mean a free finished video. Video editing software for beginners at a glance Movavi Video Editor is an intuitive video editor with customizable video templates, one-click AI tools, and hundreds of drag-and-drop effects. Available for Windows and macOS, this desktop editor works particularly well for bloggers who want to regularly publish professional-looking YouTube vlogs and reviews without spending hours on each edit. Its templates come with transitions, music, and text styles already in place. Each consists of Blocks, or short pre-edited sequences. You could use an animated intro from a template, remove a section that doesn’t suit your footage, and add other Blocks from the library. Some Blocks also come in different color schemes, so you can restyle them to match your video. There are also tools to reduce background noise and automatically reframe horizontal footage for vertical videos while keeping the subject in frame. Key features: - One-click AI for captions, reframing, noise and background removal - Hundreds of built-in effects, stickers, titles, and audio tracks Price: $19.95/month or $69.95/year. Free exports are watermarked and capped at 60 seconds. Several templates and hundreds of effects are included with the full version, with additional templates and effects available through separate subscriptions. Pros: Hover previews, built-in guidance, and free weekly editing tutorials in Movavi Ideas; AI tools without a credit system. Cons: No flexible interface customization; no cloud-based editing. CapCut is especially handy if most of your videos end up on TikTok, Instagram, or YouTube Shorts. There’s a desktop editor for Windows and macOS, alongside browser and mobile versions. The template library is a big part of CapCut’s appeal. If you’ve seen an editing trend based on a particular song or a sequence of quick cuts, there’s a chance you’ll find a template for it in CapCut. For more original edits, you can work directly on the timeline and use keyframes to animate individual elements. Auto Reframe is particularly convenient when adapting existing footage for a different aspect ratio. You can also generate captions from spoken audio and adjust their appearance to suit your video. Price: Free for basic editing. CapCut Pro costs $19.99/month or $179.99/year and includes premium assets, cloud storage, and additional AI capabilities. Pros: Extensive selection of social media templates; cloud-based project access. Cons: Many advanced tools, including Auto Reframe, require Pro; feature availability can vary between platforms. Filmora is worth considering if you want to gradually learn more elaborate editing techniques. Its desktop versions for Windows and macOS give you access to tools that go considerably beyond cutting and joining clips. Mobile apps are available, too. Say you’re putting together a product review. You can use keyframes to animate a close-up of the product or motion tracking to attach a label to it as it moves across the frame. Filmora also offers text-based editing, which can come in handy when working with lengthy recordings of someone speaking. Instead of searching through the timeline for a particular sentence, you can work with a transcript. Dynamic Captions let you create animated subtitles that follow the speech in your video. - Motion tracking to attach graphics to moving objects Price: Free with watermarked exports. Basic costs $69.99/year, while Advanced costs $79.99/year and includes 1,000 monthly AI credits. Pros: Plenty of creative tools to grow into; annual desktop subscriptions support both operating systems. Cons: Some AI features consume credits; the extensive toolset takes longer to explore. Microsoft’s Clipchamp removes much of the hassle of getting started. You can open it in a supported desktop browser or use the Windows app. One of its better features is the built-in recording tool. If you run a tech blog or make software tutorials, you can capture your screen and webcam together and edit the recording without switching programs. It’s also easy to add subtitles to a talking-head video or generate a voiceover from written text. Both tools are available for free, as is automatic silence removal. And unlike several other editors on this list, Clipchamp lets you publish a full-length HD video without buying a subscription. Price: Free with unlimited watermark-free exports at up to 1080p. Microsoft 365 Personal ($99.99/year) and Family ($129.99/year) subscribers get additional benefits, including 4K export and premium stock content. Pros: Generous free plan; recording and editing in one place. Cons: Requires a Microsoft account and an internet connection for editing. If you shoot most of your footage on an iPhone, Apple’s free iMovie is a sensible place to start. The iPhone and iPad versions are especially good at showing beginners what to film in the first place. A cooking Storyboard, for example, provides a shot list to follow as you record your recipe. Magic Movie takes a different approach: select some existing footage and the app assembles a video with music and titles. On a Mac, you’ll find a conventional editing timeline with controls for adjusting colors, stabilizing footage, and adding overlays. You can transfer an unfinished mobile project to your Mac for more detailed editing or eventually move your work to Final Cut Pro (Apple’s paid, more advanced editor). - Up to 4K video editing on compatible devices Price: Free. Pros: No subscription fees; straightforward integration with Apple devices. Cons: No built-in automatic subtitle generator; limited advanced editing controls; no Windows version. What is the best video editor for beginners? The choice largely depends on what you plan to film and how much time you want to spend editing. For lifestyle bloggers and travel vloggers, Movavi Video Editor offers a flexible way to put together videos fast using customizable templates and one-click AI. CapCut is better suited to creators who follow social media trends and mostly publish short-form content. Filmora is worth exploring if you want to experiment with animation, motion tracking, and more elaborate visual effects. If you make software tutorials or educational videos, Clipchamp lets you record your screen and edit the footage in the same program. iMovie makes sense for Apple users who want to learn the basics of editing without paying for software. Before committing to a paid plan, try editing a video similar to what you intend to publish regularly. Pay attention to how much manual work it takes to get the result you want and whether the free version’s export restrictions are acceptable to you. Is free video editing software good enough for YouTube? Yes. Clipchamp’s free 1080p exports are sufficient for most new channels, and iMovie supports 4K. Check the export restrictions before starting a longer project in other free editors. How can I make video editing for beginners easier? Make a rough cut before worrying about special effects. Remove unwanted footage first. Templates can speed up the initial edit, and automatic captions save time when you’re working with spoken content. Choosing video editor for beginners: desktop or browser? A browser editor is convenient for occasional, quick edits. If you regularly work with large recordings or want to edit offline, a desktop program is generally the more practical choice. Check its system requirements before installing it.

item.title: SALES: The 5 Best AI Tools to Maximize Your Online Meetings
item.description:
Source: PCMag
Remote work is here to stay, which means video meetings are the norm for many companies. While a day full of video calls can be tedious, the good news is that AI tools can help you better prepare for them, engage your audience, and identify clear action items. We've been covering AI in all of its modern forms, from chatbots to note-taking apps. After scouring the internet, these are the best AI meeting tools we could find to help you get the absolute most out of meetings. Some can transcribe meetings in real time, others can help you create attractive presentations, and many seamlessly integrate with the most popular video conferencing services. Make sure to click through to our full reviews of the products below to see how their AI tools fit into the larger scope of their capabilities. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The reliable Zoom Workplace combines excellent video meeting functionality with an expansive collection of AI-powered productivity tools. Canva offers an eye-popping variety of AI-powered graphic design tools that effectively help you move ideas from your imagination to the screen or print—no matter your skill level. - Friendly, intuitive interface with helpful pop-ups - Multitude of robust yet uncomplicated AI tools - Somewhat constraining for professional designers - Potentially overwhelming number of features Miro is a full-featured and unique productivity app for teams that makes it a pleasure to collaborate on, share, and present many types of work. - Excellent collaboration and presentation tools - Strong support for integrations with other apps and services With its non-linear approach and excellent video features, Prezi empowers anyone to create engaging presentations, no graphic design degree needed. - Ample selection of beautiful templates - Most plans support just two collaborators November 18, 2026: With this update, our lineup of recommended AI tools for video meetings remains unchanged. We vetted the existing picks for currency and availability. We regularly test the products on this list to evaluate new features and ensure they continue to meet expectations. We recently retested Otter as part of an update to our list of the best transcription services. Zoom's AI alerts you if somebody says your name, answers questions about what's being discussed, and even constructs ongoing summaries of meetings. After a meeting, it can critique how you presented yourself and generate transcripts for you to read over. You don't have to use these features if you don't want to, but you do need at least a Pro subscription ($14.16 per user per month, billed annually) to get more than limited in-meeting access to AI functionality. Anybody who often gets stuck in long meetings: Zoom's AI Companion shines for those times you're stuck in a long meeting. You can ask it questions and consult its ongoing summary if you lose track of the current conversation thread. Professionals: Since Zoom locks most of its AI features behind a paid tier, only professionals who spend a significant amount of time in Zoom meetings can likely justify the cost. It's probably not worth paying for if you use Zoom for the occasional personal call. Canva is all about simplifying and streamlining the graphic design process, and its suite of Canva Magic apps is a way to leverage AI to better accomplish this goal. You can use Magic Write to generate text for a presentation, while Magic Design can transform prompts into images. Alternatively, you can use Magic Animate to animate images or Magic Resize to edit them. Canva's free tier lets you use some AI features with limits, but for the full experience, you need to upgrade to Canva Pro, which costs $18 per month or $144 per year. Aspiring graphic designers: Canva's accessible interface, coupled with its robust suite of AI features, makes it an exceptional platform for trying your hand at graphic design. It provides numerous assets and templates to support your creative work. Presenters: If presenting slideshows is a key component of your job, Canva's AI tools can help you enhance your decks with easy-to-make graphics. Keeping your audience's attention is half the battle, anyway. Miro specializes in data diagramming, flowchart creation, and whiteboard collaboration. The Miro AI can summarize what's on your board, generate action items, and then convert that information into images, sticky notes, or even entire presentations. You can also ask it to rewrite any text for clarity or tone. Miro's AI features use a credit system, meaning each action you run has a cost, and its free tier gives you 10 credits per month. More expensive tiers give you more credits. Frequent collaborators: Miro is all about collaboration, making it a great tool if you and your team frequently build upon each other's ideas during and outside of meetings. Moreover, its robust integration support means you don't have to change up your established workflows. Visual learners: If you struggle to articulate your ideas during meetings, Miro lets you back up your points with clear visuals that are easy to share. Prezi helps you create visually intriguing meeting presentations using a free-form approach, allowing you to work through ideas on a canvas. But you don't need to start from scratch: Prezi AI can generate entire presentations from a prompt, which you can then customize. You can use Prezi AI for free on an AI credit basis, or sign up for Prezi's Plus plan ($19 per month, billed annually) to unlock unlimited usage. Through the Prezi desktop app, you can easily set up connections with Google Meet, Webex by Cisco, and Zoom Workplace for livestreaming and video conferencing. Non-artists: If you need to give a presentation but don't have strong creative skills, you can lean on Prezi's AI tools to create something visually compelling. Making presentations with AI is incredibly easy. People who dislike traditional slideshows: Prezi's non-linear slideshows offer a fresh approach to presentations, and its AI tools make creating them accessible. The platform gives you the freedom to present your thoughts in a way that makes sense to you. Otter excels at automatic transcription of live audio: Its AI assistant takes notes and transcribes in real time with minimal errors. Like a chatbot, it can also answer questions about what's going on if you or anyone else loses track or joins late. Otter's free tier offers decent transcription limits and supports most of the AI features above. For additional transcription minutes and more advanced features, you need to subscribe to the Pro tier ($8.33 per user per month, billed annually). You can connect Otter with Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, and Zoom Workplace. Casual collaborators: If you need transcripts from only the occasional meeting, Otter's free tier is more than capable. You get all the service's core features and up to 300 minutes of transcription per month at no cost. Re-routing through a different connecting airport can also be strategic to avoid weather issues altogether. Replacement flights must depart on the same or following day, serve the original destination or a nearby airport and be booked in the same (or lower) fare class. item.title: SALES: 11 Best Airbnbs in Stockholm for Historic Architecture, Saunas, and Beach Access
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
For a break that balances the buzz of discovering a new city with a good dose of fresh air, Stockholm’s mix of lush parks and eclectic architecture is an enduring choice. The city is formed of 14 islands, meaning you’re never too far from a waterfront to amble along. It's packed with historical charm (head to Gamla Stan to see one of Europe’s oldest medieval cobbled streets), as well as stylish boutiques and museums championing everything from Abba to the world’s best-preserved 17th-century warship. While the city is home to a slew of excellent hotels, from elegant converted townhouses to the former home of Astrid Lindgren (author of the beloved Pippi Longstocking book series), you’ll want to look to Airbnb for a real home-from-home vibe. These 11 excellent rentals throughout the city and its outskirts balance top-notch amenities with the freedom that only comes with a private booking. True to Nordic form, there’s a clutch of homes with their own sauna and steam rooms, and all have either sea or skyline views. Below, the best Airbnbs in Stockholm to book for a weekend of weaving through medieval streets, gallery hopping, and lots of cinnamon buns. We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor. Our top picks: Why we love it: Historic architecture, prime location, dedicated workspaceSubverting traditional Scandi minimalist sensibilities, this cool retreat in the hip heart of Södermalm channels a moody, more underground kind of charm. On the top floor, light-flooded, open-plan living areas are packed with rich, creamy furnishings and crisp architectural lines—multiple previous guests say that this is one of the most stylish homes they’ve ever stayed in. Downstairs, two tranquil bedrooms are carved directly into the exposed natural rock, so you can sleep beneath historic vaulted ceilings after a long day skipping from sight to sight. On that note: Södermalm is an eclectic area of town, with plenty of vintage shops and wine bars, after which you can hole up in this cocooning, cave-like retreat, as though you’re stepping into your own secret—and very stylish—bunker. Neighborhood: Södermalm Things to do nearby: Fotografiska, Riddarholm Church, Stockholm City Museum Why we love it: Forest access, indoor fireplace, outdoor gas grillBlink, and you might miss this off-grid, A-frame cabin, hidden among a thick swathe of pine trees. It’s worth searching for: Once you make your way through the foliage, you’ll find a truly wonderful Swedish escape for two. The glass-fronted structure invites in all of the elements, while inside, it’s time to switch off—there’s a crackling open hearth where you can grill all of your meals, and precious little noise other than the rustle of wind through the canopy. Fair warning: There’s a very rustic toilet and seasonal shower about a 30-second walk down the forest path, so if you’re not a DIY fan, perhaps look elsewhere. Nonetheless, for more adventurous sorts, the trade-off means absolute tranquility surrounded by happily grazing sheep and twinkly starry night skies—all within a hop and a skip of the capital. Neighborhood: Värmdö Things to do nearby: Lillsved Beach, Buddharama Temple, Stora Sandön Why we love it: Historic warehouse, steps from the lake, wood-burning fireplaceWood-beamed ceilings, clattering floors, a muted color scheme, and a signature bright exterior welcome you in from the cold—this former warehouse just oozes 19th-century charm the moment you round the corner. Better yet, it’s totally massive, sprawling across three roomy floors, with a prime spot perched right on the peaceful banks of Åkers canal. A snazzy and social kitchen space opens onto a central island and a fireplace, where all the family will want to gather. When it’s time to bed down, there are cozy curtained sleeping nooks and an additional attic dormitory, adding a playful, rustic vibe. You can rent canoes from host Cecile to paddle down the canal, or jump on an e-bike to explore the surrounding nature reserves. When you return, fire up the outdoor grill and gather around the dining table for a long dinner with more endless views. Neighborhood: Norrö-Stava Things to do nearby: Prästfjärden lake, Näsudden nature reserve, Åkersbro walking trails Why we love it: Sea views, sauna, hot tubThis joyfully bobbing houseboat turns the gray blue waters of the Baltic into something akin to your own front lawn—and it does so just 15 minutes from the heady sights of central Stockholm. Panoramic floor-to-ceiling glass means you feel that you’re virtually out on the water—and, of course, you can dive straight into the lake from your bedroom deck. Dry off and hop into the private wood-fired sauna to warm up. Hop off the boat, and you can sunbathe on the jetty, cook up some local catches on the barbecue, or jump into the complimentary canoe. All in all, this is an idyllic waterside playground that active types will love. Neighborhood: Boo Things to do nearby: Kringelgården bakery, Saltsjöbadens golf course, Artipelag Why we love it: Sauna, beach access, pet-friendlyExpect some truly good seascape ASMR when you stay here—you’re so close to the water you can hear the waves rolling onto the shore right from the porch. Grab the kayak from the cupboard and head down to the beach to make the most of this beautiful location. It’s a short drive from the home to Stockholm’s city center, but you’re rewarded with much serenity and glorious views instead. For those seeking a secluded family stay, this is the place. Neighborhood: Tyresö Things to do nearby: Sandholmarna nature preserve, Tyresta nature reserve, Lilla beach Why we love it: Wood stove, sauna, beach accessThis spacious waterside cottage is not in Stockholm’s city center, but by compromising on a 30-minute commute into town, you gain something really special. The owners took the original 130-year-old structure down piece by piece, rebuilding it on their own property. It was worth the effort. Now, it lies surrounded by pine trees in a nature reserve beside a sparkling, clear lake, with the sea just a few steps further in the other direction. A large porch provides the spot for barbecue dinners and sunbathing sessions in the summer, and there are two spas within walking distance for those looking for their Scandi sweat fix—the sea-facing Skepparholmen Spa, and Japanese onsen-style Yasuragi. But you don't have to head that far, as the property has its own sauna. Stay in as long as you can muster, then cool off by jumping in the lake—something all the more satisfactory in the winter months. Neighborhood: Boo Things to do nearby: Boobadet Beach, Nyckelvikens wildlife refuge, Sushi Bar Namiyama Why we love it: Rooftop views, beach access, pet-friendlyA previous guest says this flat has a New York City vibe, and we can see why—the interior space is small but stylish, with an industrial bent and views all over the coolest part of Stockholm from the balcony. It’s on the top floor of this apartment block, so the vistas can’t be beat. It’s been a winner for those on work trips, thanks to superfast WiFi and a dedicated workspace, and, unusually for Airbnb stays, you can bring your dog too. Neighborhood: Södermalm Things to do nearby: Liljeholmsviken waterfront, Högalid Church, Skinnarviksberget Why we love it: Steam room, in-unit washer/dryer, fully equipped kitchenFor an Airbnb stay that’s as close to checking into a luxury hotel as possible, look to this plush apartment right in the city center. The whole place is brand new, and no expense has been spared on the fittings—there are genuine oak floorboards, Italian travertine surfaces, underfloor heating, and a slew of top-notch furniture, plus little touches such as a shower seat and a gloriously powerful rainfall shower. The best bit is the steam room; there’s no better way to decompress after a long flight or a blustery autumnal walk by the river. Neighborhood: Vasastan Things to do nearby: Vanadislunden park, Odenplan plaza, Swedish Museum of Natural History Why we love it: Proximity to metro, private patio, in-unit washer/dryerIf dopamine itself could be characterized as a building, it’d be this one. The place (all 300 square feet of it) is pure joy from top to bottom—with a pink-tiled kitchen, mint-green bathroom, and cozy bedroom nook with yellow walls and blue candy-striped bedding. Cheery artworks add a final flourish. Despite its bijou size, there’s room for two more guests on the pullout bed, and there’s a patio with twinkly fairy lights to sit out on sunny afternoons with a book, a glass of wine, or both. Neighborhood: Älvsjö Things to do nearby: Älvsjö Forest Nature Preserve, Herrängens Gård, Långbro park Why we love it: Beach access, sauna, kayakForget your average homely fisherman’s cottage—this home here, on the cusp of the lake in the city’s swish Stocksund neighborhood, marks a newer, more modern breed of lake house. It’s chic as anything you’ll find in the city, with smooth, polished concrete floors and knotty pine walls finished with a moody, cocooning interior palette. Sweeping glass windows make the most of the beautiful views that stretch over the water and right to the city as it twinkles on the other side. Grab the kayak and spend an afternoon bobbing on the lake, then stop in for a well-deserved sweat session in the private sauna. Neighborhood: Stocksund Things to do nearby: Restaurang Hemma, Svanholmsparken park, Swedish Museum of Natural History Why we love it: Wood-burning fireplace, Aesop toiletries, garden viewThis traditional Swedish apartment has had a modern facelift recently. Now it pairs gorgeous original features, including imposing 10-foot-high ceilings and whitewashed floorboards, with a sleek new kitchen and selection of cool designer furniture pieces. There's also a truly cloudlike sofa just made for cozy nights in. The surrounding streets are just as cool as the interiors; this home is smack dab in SoFo—by far Stockholm’s trendiest district—so you're just one street over from a clutch of the best of the city’s bar, restaurant, and café scene. Neighborhood: Södermalm Things to do nearby: Fotografiska, Stockholm City Museum, Vitabergsparken park This gallery was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller UK.

REI’s take on the Alpha hoody is soft, warm, and has a better layering fit than others we’ve tested. Plus, it’s cheaper than most other hoodies on the market thanks to REI’s house-brand price modeling. Inspiration from the couch might be the final push someone needs to take the plunge and commit to their next trip. This coffee-table-worthy book covers 50 of the best hiking trails in North, Central, and South America, ranging from six months on the Pacific Crest Trail to overnight treks in Peru. Free Fly’s recently upgraded blend of bamboo fibers and polyester is more durable and pill-resistant than previous versions, without losing the brand’s signature softness.
