item.title: SALES: The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert
item.description:
Source: Eater
The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world. The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult. We update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30. New to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience. Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023. As Jonathan Nunn wrote in his guide to north London’s best-value restaurants, “Durak, a tantuni salonu run by Dogan Yesil on West Green Road, is the superior late night snack template.” Only the tantuni, a speciality which originates in the city of Mersin on the southern coast of Turkey, is served here. Beef is boiled, seasoned with the likes of tomato, pul biber, sumac, and cumin and subsequently fried in cotton oil before being loaded, meat juices aplenty, inside a thin lavash with chopped parsley, tomato, and onion. It is then given a pleasing bend before being eaten; a selection of high-acid accompaniments — pickled chiles, lemon — provide the necessary cut-through. Best for: A snack on the way home after a long day. Mukaddes Yadikar’s restaurant near Walthamstow Central station opened in London in summer 2017. It was London’s first strictly Uyghur restaurant, and has become perhaps E17’s finest neighborhood restaurant. To start, go for the Chaomian, a stir-fry of short noodle snippets wokked with chunks of beef, spring onion, and tomato. Third, and most importantly, get the signature da pan ji (“big plate chicken”): a remarkably deep, savoury, and spicy chicken and potato stew, teeming with Sichuan peppercorns, served with flat hand-pulled noodles. This is a warm, homely, and treasured space to eat in east London. Best for: Casual dinner with a group. This small Stoke Newington cafe seriously overdelivers, preparing some of London’s best American diner-style smash burgers, Nashville hots, playful samosas, and the inimitable chicken makhani sandwich come the weekend, with a solid core menu for weekday visitors. Its sweet offering isn’t half bad either; cookies are particularly excellent, as is the seasonal ice cream from Crabtree and co-founder Feroz Gajia in warmer months. Must-try dish: Do not miss the ingenious creme brulee cookie, developed by pastry chef Chloe-Rose Crabtree from a recipe by Los Angeles’s Dough and Arrow. And the makhani chicken bun at weekends. Open for: Lunch and dinner on weekends, dinner only during the week Eater London’s Restaurant of the Year 2022 comprises three discrete yet intertwined endeavors. Downstairs in the basement kitchen, George Jephson butchers whole animals, repurposing them as immaculate charcuterie, while upstairs, chef Mike Murphy uses excellent ingredients to prepare simple plates that lean French and southern European — think trout poached in butter with roe and sorrel; or a roast game bird with quince and bitter leaves. Sommeliers Tom Beattie and Fran Roberts, the duo behind the wine importer bearing both names, run the bar and the floor with a small team. Cadet is a wine bar, a restaurant, a charcutier, and a shopfront; it feels French and it feels London; and, from the moment it opened, it has always felt just right. Must-try dish: Pate en croute. This diminutive Vietnamese shop on Hackney’s Graham Road serves one of the city’s best sandwiches — inside one of the city’s best baguettes. Although the spot has just one table and three or four seats, it’s difficult to think of warmer hospitality than at Bánh Mì Hội-An. The duo behind the counter prepare fresh sandwiches to go, and while the pork classic is excellent, don’t sleep on the turmeric-heavy fried catfish on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays; fragrant with coriander, mayo, fermented chile paste, sriracha, and pickled vegetables, it is an object lesson in flavor, texture, and balance. Best for: Takeaway lunch. Ex-Noma sommelier Yukiyasu Kaneko’s wine bar, set in a cozy space beneath a railway arch close to London Fields, may yet become the new template for natural wine bars, a category that has grown a little tired and derivative. Few other businesses can rival Yuki’s assured sense of self and pleasing ambience. An extensive (and fairly priced) list includes highlights from the Jura, Savoie, and Loire regions, as well as bottles from elsewhere in the Old World. Food is secondary but not an afterthought, with snacky dishes such as eggs with tahini, house-made potato crisps dressed with sansho pepper, cured beet tops, silken tofu with mushrooms, and made-to-order beef tartare. Must-try dish: Ask Yuki for his best wines from the Jura or the Savoie. These days, London has no shortage of excellent new-age wine bars. It’s been a signature category in the city since the days of P. Franco and the likes of Terroirs before. But in more recent times, spots like Cadet, Hector’s, and Yuki Bar have raised the standard of wine bars sharply. At Goodbye Horses, which opened in the second part of 2024 (and where I enjoyed one of my favorite nights out last year), sommelier Nathalie Nelles oversees one of the most interesting wine lists in the city. Nelles has a penchant for excellent French wines from the Jura, Loire, and Burgundy. Go in the evening to enjoy a selection of small plates, which might include an avant-garde beef tartare, some carefully arranged crostini-like toasts, and a cheese plate. But you’re here to drink, really, and to take in the quite extraordinary interior, hand-painted curtains and long, organically shaped wooden bar — which lend the room a World of Interiors vibe in the best way. Must-try: Complex savagnins from the Jura, elegant chenin blancs from the Loire Valley, grower Champagnes, and a mix of modern and classic wines from regal Burgundian producers. East Ham is home to London’s largest Kerala community and its greatest concentration of South Indian restaurants. The pick of them is Thattukada, run by chef-owners Biju and Preeti Gopinath. Curries and roasts have a depth of flavor and spicing that belie their simple descriptions, and they should be mopped up with crisp parottas or snow-white appams. But it’s the legendary fries that are unmissable: half a chicken cut into segments, then aggressively and skillfully fried with chiles and crispy onions; little netholi (anchovies) cooked and eaten whole; or battered mussels that pop thrillingly in the mouth. Must-try dish: Get the mussel fry. This elegantly designed wine club beneath a Haggerston railway arch now firmly belongs in the top bracket of (French) restaurants in London. Chef Seb Myers and his modern-ish, playful take on French country cooking fits perfectly with the fascinating and broad wine list owned by patron Jonathan Alphandery. With dishes such as a red mullet tartine; grilled leeks vinaigrette with Tunworth cheese; a duck offal choux farcis; and mackerel with coco beans and greens; as well as a caramel tart with blue cheese, Planque has nearly everything that makes a great modern European restaurant great. Best for: Pairing some of London’s cleverest cooking with some of the best wine in the city. Open for: Lunch and dinner, with brunch on weekends Since Cafe Cecilia opened in 2021, it has maintained a steady flow of plaudits from all the coolest places, in part because of chef-owner Max Rocha’s connection to the world of fashion (father John and sister Simone are designers). However, there’s a surfeit of substance as well as style in this stark, minimalist cafe-bistro. And playfulness, too, seen in the likes of recreations of chicken Kievs or deep-fried bread-and-butter pudding in a pool of cold custard. Rocha and his staff are direct descendaents of the ingredients-obsessed tradition of St. John, the River Cafe, and Quo Vadis. Like peer Anna Tobias’s cooking at Cafe Deco, Rocha’s can be colored a bit beige, but it deserves the attention it has received. Must-try dish: Do not miss the steak and chips with peppercorn sauce, nor fruit tart at dessert. This quaint place close to King’s Cross hasn’t been open long, but has been a conversation starter the likes of which the London restaurant scene hasn’t seen for years. Chef and Belfastman Hugh Corcoran’s sub-20-seater venue is open only at lunchtime (midday and 2 p.m. sittings are offered), reservations must be made via the restaurant’s landline (or postcard, honestly), it is cash-only, and the wine menu is all kept inside the faintly grumpy, periodically affable proprietor’s head. You can skip the starters (save, perhaps, the homemade soda bread and butter); just head straight to the mains, where you might find a slice of game bird pie with mash, a portion of braised guinea fowl with cabbage, or a fantastic rendition of a Dublin classic — coddle: boiled, peppery white sausages in a salty broth with root vegetables and lots of allium. This place eschews everything that the London restaurant industry has become, while bringing forth some (if not all) of the good things it once offered. And you can say, “I was there then.” Best for: Going back in time. The area around Euston station is replete with no-frills, delicious places to eat. This little Malaysian basement setup from chef Sugen Gopal on Doric Way may be the best. Two pieces of freshly made, high-moisture roti canai — to eat in or take away — are best served with curry dal. Roti King has a few other locations throughout London as well. Know before you go: The new online queueing system makes for a seamless experience. Chef Ed Wilson’s hearty French Italian menu is a showcase for his own personal love of food. To eat here is to share that passion, especially now with an increased emphasis on fresh pasta and spectacular comfort food. Wines are predominantly natural and biodynamic. Illustrated wine posters, art, and curios on whitewashed brick walls also make the two relaxed dining rooms on Columbia Road among London’s most handsome and cool. Vibe check: This place has the city’s smallest and most beautiful bathrooms — among the very first to use Aesop, too. At the late chef Kate Armah’s outstanding neighborhood Ghanaian restaurant in east London, the sharing platter — which includes tsofi, chicken wings, kebabs, plantains, and more — might be the definition of generosity in hospitality. Other highlights here include akonfem (guinea fowl), red red (fried plantain with black eye bean stew and gari foto), and any of the soups, which come served with choice of starchy sides such as fufu, kenkey, kokonte, or rice. Vibe check: As the venue of choice for many visiting musicians and performers, Kate’s might be London’s least-appreciated celebrity restaurant. There is no shortage of decent pizza in this town, but reliably excellent New York-style slices are harder to come by. Tom Vincent’s Vincenzo’s, which has been a bona fide IYKYK destination in Bushey, Watford for the last half decade, made its arrival in central London at the end of 2025 and since then has been treating the city to an excellent roster of classics and innovative pies. There are cheese, tomato, and pepperoni pizzas, all featuring low-moisture mozzarella, good tomato sauce, and a delightfully crisp base. U.S. colleagues might even admire the resistance to tip dip. Beyond the classics, look out for a spanakopita slice featuring feta, creamed spinach, and a Scotch bonnet honey; and the lesser-seen, thicker-based grandma pie for the heads, sometimes topped with vodka sauce, other times with pepperoni and hot honey. Best for: Probably the best pizza slice in town. After a refurbishment of both kitchen and premises, this haven on Farringdon Road is back to the form that has made it one of the most essential of the city’s essential kitchens in recent years. Chef Nick Bramham’s cooking now leans more towards the Aegean, with the likes of giouvarlakia bringing herbed meatballs bobbing in avgolemono. The menu will change weekly and will travel across southern Europe, but look out for Bramham’s clever riffs on BLTs, lobster rolls, and perfectly seasoned pasta dishes, after peerless gildas, before flawless sour cherry cannoli. Must-try dish: When Nick does pasta or Nick does a sandwich, you must order it. Clerkenwell’s Sushi Tetsu might be the hardest reservation in London. It also pound-for-pound serves the best (value) sushi in the city. To observe Toru Takahashi’s knife skills and to eat his omakase menu while receiving Harumi Takahashi’s gently flawless hospitality (the two are married) is to experience one of London’s most complete and completely brilliant restaurants. Know before you go: There are only seven seats in the restaurant, all at the sushi counter. Joké Bakare’s small, two-story central London venue is no secret to anyone interested in restaurants: The chef’s modern recreations of classic dishes from Nigeria and the broader West African region have earned recognition from across the globe, including from the Michelin guide, which awarded Chishuru a star. As well as the chef’s immense presence, inventiveness, and ability to convey her love of food, the brilliance of Chishuru’s menu is rooted in age-old practices of fermentation, which lend many of the dishes a deep and lasting umami. It’s there in dishes like beef sirloin and dawadawa short rib with Tokyo turnip and a bitter leaf sauce, as well as grilled guinea fowl breast with celeriac cake, jalapeño, and egusi sauce. Must-try dishes: Be sure to try Bakare’s jollof rice, and leave room for dessert. Given the pace at which restaurants are modernizing and as the internationality of food becomes ever more commonplace, the Ledbury’s tablecloths and Franco-modern European style might be classified as old-school-ish. But that would be to ignore the level of craft and conscientious sourcing, and its application of Japanese ingredients and techniques in dishes like Cornish bluefin otoro with miyagawa and black sesame; or veal sweetbread with parsnip, liquorice, pear, and sansho pepper. And, finally, to consider the Ledbury a relic would be to overlook the profound influence chef-owner Brett Graham has had on the professional development of many of London’s best modern chefs — from BRAT to the Clove Club and beyond. Best for: Birthdays, anniversaries, and one of the most special fine-dining experiences in the city. Chef Meedu Saad’s hotly-anticipated Soho restaurant feels all at once brand new, a fixture of Soho and primed to remain in situ for years to come. Super 8, the group behind it and celebrated venues like Kiln, Brat, and Mountain, has a knack for creating the restaurants that Londoners (and tourists) really want, before they know they want it. Impala embodies the qualities that give the group its edge — a buzzy, handsome dining room, thoughtfully curated playlists, attentive and cool service, plus clever dishes prepared with fine, carefully-sourced produce. The group also promotes its best talent to give them a platform; in Saad, backed by development chef Songsoo Kim, they have a star. This north Londoner, British Egyptian chef is cooking his own food: North African leaning with French and modern British accents, most of it over hot coals or from a wood-fired oven. Try the aish balady with Tunisian harissa, ftira with egg, a grilled squid and green leaf salad, sheftalia, molokhia with lamb, Cantonese-ish-style roast duck with fig sauce, or an elegant pilaf. And save room for the one dessert: a pistachio and date custard tart. Must-try dish: Cantonese-style roast duck with molasses and fig sauce. (Get it with the pilaf.) Shuko Oda’s little bar in Soho is among London’s most acclaimed Japanese restaurants. Over a long, blond wooden counter, chefs calmly and politely pass hot bowls of steaming broth containing noodles made on-site, topped with proteins like tempura prawn or smoked mackerel, or seasonal green vegetables from Sussex farm Namayasai. The traditional Japanese breakfast is the most steadying in London. Know before you go: The specials board of small plates changes every day and exhibits some of the city’s best modern British cooking. Bar Italia remains one of London’s most precious institutions, a relic of the mid-20th century sitting indomitably on Soho’s Frith Street. More than almost anywhere else in the capital, Soho is a victim of change, fads, and nonsensical restaurants. (True story: A half decade ago this same street played host to a venue called Flavour Bastard.) But Bar Italia never changes. And for that, we must be grateful. Its consistency and sense of self is what makes it so steadying and reassuring in a world of flux and uncertainty. At Bar Italia you always know your espresso will be bitter, your Peroni will be cold, and your bacon ciabatta will be better than almost anything else you can get in this storied but spoiled patch of the city. Best for: An iconic, reliable breakfast and espresso. For my money, Ikoyi may be the choicest special occasion venue in the city. Chef Jeremy Chan and restaurateur Iré Hasan-Odukale’s venue has evolved since its inception in St. James’s in 2017. It now occupies a sleek location in the bowels of 180 The Strand and has matured accordingly, elevating the food yet further to match its fancy new surroundings. While it is still philosophically rooted in the culinary traditions and flavor profiles of Nigeria and the West African region, Ikoyi is now an archetype of the Ultra-Modern European genre. Recent meals have featured the seductive savory deliciousness of Chan’s signature smoked jollof rice, and the precise application of spice and chile heat to immaculately cooked protein will blow you away, whether it’s sweetbread suya, dry-aged turbot, or charcoal-grilled lobster. A special restaurant, deserving of its two Michelin-starred status. Best for: A true blowout dinner. Gerrard Street’s Cantonese institution needs little introduction. Wong Kei is a decades-old London restaurant famous for its multistory dining room, roast meats (duck, char siu), wontons, red-ringed plates, and the now-cult (if much overstated) brusque service. Its enduring appeal — in spite of newer, trendier, regionally diverse restaurants in central London’s Chinatown — is its faithfulness to the traditions of dependable and delicious Cantonese cooking in the U.K., the stuff of a bygone era. In other words, it’s a giant, 500-seat living monument to a time before bubble waffles and Instagram-first openings. Best for: A nostalgic UK-Cantonese meal with a group. Chef Normah Abd Hamid and her family team offer a Malaysian comfort menu that makes the restaurant one of the best in the city from a nook of a unit in Queensway Market. Sour, hot assam pedas; roti to rival London’s King in Euston; and beef rendang or nasi lemak to go alongside. Normah’s is quaint and Normah is brilliant; this remains one of central London’s best restaurants to visit with a small group of friends and one to take out-of-towners visiting the city. Know before you go: The food is halal, and no alcohol is allowed on site. Mayfair’s two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of a few places in London that manages to straddle the line between celebrity hype and quality cooking. Tandoori masala lamb chops, chicken butter masala, and the trademark wild muntjac biryani remain standouts 13 years after it arrived on Albemarle Street. The prices match the level of cooking and the illustrious surroundings, making this one for special occasions. Best for: Special occasions, atmosphere, and some of the finest curries in the city. Together with Saikei, this is one of the great places in London to eat dim sum — particularly, with a big group on a Sunday lunchtime for the whole experience, driving out to the Docklands, walking up the wooden staircase to above a mixed martial arts gym, and putting your name down among the dozens of others to wait for a table. Once inside and seated, it’s a procession of tea and food. Be sure to order extra of the prawn and chive dumplings, and the special fried cheung fun with XO sauce (one of the best rice noodle dishes in the city). You might plump for sui mai, tripe, or some ribs. Barely anything you choose will disappoint. And from there, it might be a selection of sticky-sweet roast meats, or a Cantonese-style steamed seabass with ginger and spring onions and rice to share for the table. There is no way you’ll leave unsatisfied; lunch at Yi-Ban is pure nourishment. Best for: Sunday lunch with a group (and plane spotting at City Airport). There’s something lazily obvious about including the Ritz on a list of essential restaurants in London, but credit where credit’s due. The chef in charge comes fully garlanded: John Williams MBE is the master of niche, old-school French fine dining, delivering dishes of exceptional precision, yet never at the expense of deliciousness. Despite much frippery and eye-watering expense, when you get down to the brass tacks of a meal at the Ritz, it’s really quite simple: immaculately seasoned ingredients, assembled into balanced dishes, cooked adroitly. That’s true across the menu, but nowhere more so than in the Dorset crab with creme fraiche and Imperial caviar; filet of veal with white asparagus and lovage; the classic beef Wellington; and the theatrical crepe suzette. Know before you go: The restaurant will make sure you comply with the formal dress code. A treasure. Unmoved by the comings and goings of trends, Bermondsey’s 40 Maltby St is a 40-cover answer to the question, pejorative as it may often be: What is British food? Steve Williams is a chef’s chef, cited by James Lowe, Brett Graham, and Florence Knight in their top five in the city. Raef Hodgson of distributor Gergovie Wines — which features low-intervention styles — runs the front-of-house without hubris. Recent dishes included winners such as pork schnitzel with raw celeriac, mustard, and braised potatoes, onion, and thyme, or a chestnut and brown sugar meringue. Know before you go: Check Instagram for the menu, which always features an in-joke or two. This vast restaurant dining room sits quite inexplicably on the ground floor of a Holiday Inn Express budget hotel just off the A102 on the south exit of the Blackwall Tunnel. But this is a destination dining room of tremendous pedigree. A mid-length, high-quality dim sum menu features a must-try fried prawn and Chinese chive number that stakes a fair claim to being the best single-bite hot item in the city — a crispy, fatty, sweet, salty umami nugget. Among the noodle plates to share, king prawns are excellent, with the noodles taking on the requisite smoke from the wok, seasoned judiciously. Saikei is a close-to-perfect family and group dining experience. Best for: Sunday lunch, preferably with a large group. Open for: Dinner to late night during the week, lunch to late night on weekends In his guide to the city’s best East African restaurants, Riaz Phillips says Adulis’s “palatial setting has to make it one of the finest east African and Eritrean restaurants in the capital.” The dark wooden fixtures give every meal here a sense of occasion. The restaurant is well-suited to solo or group dining, with a menu offering selections for one, two, four, and eight persons. Look out for kwanta fitfit, smoked, dried beef with green chile and injera; zilzl assa, grilled red snapper seasoned with Eritrean herbs; and the entire range of vegetarian and vegan stews, comprising spinach, beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all eaten with more of the excellent, subtly tangy, and moreish injera. Best for: A special occasion with vegetarians and vegans. Open for: Dinner on weeknights, brunch through dinner on weekends The second branch for this south London institution, Nandine — “kitchen” in Kurdish — is run by Pary Baban, husband Pola, and sons Rang and Raman. During the day it serves a menu of brunch dishes, meze, and intricate pastries. Technicolored and abundant meze platters served in the evening include kubba (minced beef and rice patties), onion dolma, and qawarma. Pastries like borek, made with a Kurdish pastry called galgali, and baklava are not to be missed. Best for: Go for brunch and get the meze, for yourself. Bruce Poole’s Wandsworth Common institution is best summed up thus: technique, decadence, and salt. There’s skill and execution here that no longer feels commonplace in restaurants in London (explained, perhaps in part, by how out-of-London it feels). It’s classical in almost every sense; the dining room has the breezy, impressionist art-covered air of a destination neighborhood bistro in which Michelin’s inspectors would feel welcome. But what it lacks in new-wave imagination over the course of a meal, it makes up for in professionalism and elan. My favorite dish during a recent visit was a “homemade” (you’ve gotta shout about these things in buzzy Wandsworth) cavatelli with duck and morteau sausage ragu, showered with Parmesan: rich, moreish, sumptuous — a flawless small plate of pasta. Best for: Special occasions, especially including a glass or two of vintage Champagne. Possibly London’s best Jamaican jerk shop. On the edge of Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park, with a smoky aroma detectable from many hundred meters, this stark room is dedicated to one thing: immaculately, judiciously seasoned protein grilled without remorse. The age of these oil drums and the time-honored expertise of chef Murphy Lawrence and his team result in jerked pork belly, chicken, goat, and even lobster, all penetrated with smoke and lifted by allspice, Scotch bonnet, and salt. Tasty Jerk is a heady, intoxicating, and remarkably good-value eating experience. Know before you go: Buy a bottle of the home-made pepper sauce to take away, but use with caution and keep it in the fridge. Fascinated by British meats and Thai cooking preparations, restaurateur Ben Chapman opened this homage to northern Thailand on Brewer Street in Soho 10 years ago this year. It has always been a dynamic showcase for rare-breed British meat in spicy, piquant laabs, Cornish dayboat fish in bright seafood curries, and complex, herbaceous salads (a mix of British leaves and Thai herbs), the like of which are seldom found anywhere in the capital. Almost all of the cooking here is done not with electricity or gas, but over charcoal. Must-try dish: Claypot glass noodles. Don’t skip the wine list. Despite the proximity of France to Britain, the restaurant traditions and contemporary scenes have little in common. There is just something – the je ne sais quoi – about bistros in France which isn’t often found in venues on this side of the channel. But there are those who manage to recreate the mythos and romanticism of the bistro-proper. Chef Henry Harris’s longstanding practice in the field of French cooking lends him a rare level of expertise. His Bouchon Racine sits above a pub close to Farringdon station, and it feels like a bistro – tables are close, there’s little in the way of frippery, the menu is written out in chalk on a blackboard, which is moved around the dining room. It’s difficult to choose, but a good place to start is with a plate of paté or terrine, followed by one of the finest versions of rabbit in mustard sauce; confit de canard; or a côte de boeuf to share. It would be rude not to finish with a crème caramel and a pate of cheese. Best for: Lapin à la moutarde, French bistro classics. Open for: Lunch and dinner during the week (but check opening hours; reservations by email only.) The artist Peter Doig is scheduled to reopen McGlynn’s, the famous King’s Cross pub he purchased last year, early in 2027. In advance of that, Doig, his daughter Celeste who oversees operations, and former River Cafe chef Harry McKenzie have been trialling dishes and menus at a space just off City Road. The results: some of the best seasonal British cooking the city has had to offer in 2026. There could be featherlight cheese puffs, house morcilla with roasted red peppers, a plate of house-made cavatelli with borlotti beans or fresh girolles to start. A recent lamb stew in a medley of heritage grains (barley, emer, and others) with turnip and carrots signalled the arrival of autumn in the most comforting of fashions. For dessert, there are baked apples with luxurious, vanilla-heavy custard, or simply a small plate of peerless oat cookies. Best for: The most delicious, hyper-seasonal cooking in the city right now.

item.title: SALES: The Best Places to Go in Central and South America 2027
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
This is my fourth year leading our guide to the Best Places to Go in Central and South America, and each time I’m in awe of the final result—our list for 2027 is no exception. We’re talking about a region where the Pacific, the Atlantic, and the Caribbean converge; where the Andes reach for the Amazon; and where strings of puffy volcanoes and postcard-worthy islands stud the map like jewels. Within it all there are thriving cities where cultures ancient and modern collide head-on, and small towns that are timeless in a way that feels increasingly rare. It may be a fool’s errand to distill all this wonder into a list of just 10 destinations. But the places below, as singular or more broadly representative as they may be, are the region’s answer to how we are traveling right now. For example, a pioneering set of travel specialists are ready to bring you to eco-lodges that are tucked in the untamed jungle of Guyana for wildlife sightings and citizen science experiences that will broaden your understanding of the only (official) English-speaking country in South America. If you’re looking for a sport to pick up, Preá on Brazil’s northeast coast has an open invitation on kitesurfing, the wind-driven sport this fishing village has long been known for—and the reason a set of quietly luxurious boutique hotels have been cropping up within driving distance of the rolling sand dunes of Jericoacoara National Park. If wine is what moves you, then Chile’s Central Valley should be your next stop: A slew of new culinary experiences and interesting bottles from up-and-coming winemakers make this Santiago-adjacent region the trip to take in 2027. There’s also next-gen wellness in Costa Rica, quintessential expedition cruises in Ecuador, offseason trekking in Argentina, and so much more. Get ready to max out that PTO. These are the Best Places to Go in Central and South America in 2027. —Megan Spurrell This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here. Go for: new jungle stays, ancestral wellness experiences, and a next-level approach to ecotourism Half a century ago Costa Rica helped pioneer a new model of travel in the Monteverde Cloud Forest that would come to be known as ecotourism. Today the free-spirited residents of Monteverde, three hours northwest of the capital, San José, are once again redefining responsible travel—yet now the goal extends beyond minimizing tourism’s footprint to actively restoring ecosystems, supporting local communities, and forging deeper connections between visitor and place. That ethos is embodied by Artista Villas, a collection of 10 swish bungalows in a reforestation site at Hotel Belmar. Guests at the carbon-neutral property, which opened in June, engage with the surrounding jungle using in-room art kits, meet visiting artists and filmmakers at the property’s Cervecería Belmar, forest bathe in the mountain at Artista-owned Savia nature reserve, and learn about the source of their meals at Finca Madre Tierra. Calling this new form of regenerative travel ecotourism feels too small to capture its weight. As conventional foreign-owned resorts proliferate along the nearby Gulf of Papagayo, Monteverde and the surrounding highlands continue to chart a different course. In March 2027 the working ranch and private reserve Hacienda Montezuma, located beneath the Tenorio Volcano (and normally reserved for exclusive buyouts), will launch the first in a series of wellness retreats bookable for up to 15 people. These will feature local practitioners leading equine therapy, meditation, and forest walks—all rooted in ancestral traditions. The region is also transitioning to a deforestation-free coffee model that is reshaping how one of Costa Rica's most important crops is both grown and experienced by visitors on educational tours. —Mark Johanson Go for: chef-led experiences, new Cachapoal Valley bungalows, and up-and-coming wine scenes Chile’s central wine valleys have long been defined by their vines—emerald rows sprawling along riverbanks, blanketing a terrain reminiscent of the Mediterranean, yet hemmed between towering Andes and a thrashing Pacific. Recently, dynamic chefs from Santiago have begun adding their touch to the region, crafting new culinary tours and elevating the work of emerging bodegas and wineries. Kurt Schmidt is among them. He first rose to fame crafting nine-course tasting menus at Santiago’s 99 Restaurante, built around the traditional foodways of Chilean viticultural regions. In 2027 he’ll be teaming up with the rural tourism cooperative Ruta de los Abastos (“The Supply Route”) on menu-to-territory day tours that will begin at 99 and expand out to wine valleys like Huasco, Maule, and Aconcagua, where Schmidt has spent years building relationships with vintners, cheesemakers, foragers, and fisherfolk (later multiday itineraries are in the works). Conveniently, Santiago lies just south of the Maipo Valley, which is famed for bold Cabernet Sauvignons and also home to the striking new Centro del Vino from Concha y Toro, Latin America’s largest wine producer. The 129,000-square-foot facility features contemporary art installations, barrel-side tasting rooms, and an interactive wine museum, plus access to manicured gardens and (for an additional fee) the 19th-century mansion of founder Don Melchor. If you have days to spare, consider heading three hours south to the Cachapoal Valley. Here, Chile’s most extravagant wine hotel, VIK, expanded in 2026 with eight glass-mirrored bungalows and an art-filled wellness center. Five cabins are next, set to open in an oak forest on the property, where winemaker Cristián Vallejo ages natural wine in clay amphorae. Continuing south, you can explore the next generation of experimental and low-intervention vino emerging from the neighboring Maule and Itata valleys, where Millennial and Gen Z winemakers are injecting fresh energy into one of South America's oldest regions at bodegas like González Bastías and Carter Mollenhauer. Add it all up and it makes for an epic wine country road trip. As if that weren’t enough to keep you busy, know that excellent vino isn’t the only reason to dedicate your big vacation to Chile this year. Once you wrap up in Santiago, consider hopping over to Rapa Nui (Easter Island) for some extreme set-jetting. This remote Chilean territory in the Southeastern Pacific is the backdrop of Academy Award winner Martin McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, and it’s sure to become a rising star on more travelers’ itineraries this year. —Mark Johanson Go for: new conservation-minded cruises, stargazing experiences, and an endless parade of wildlife The Galápagos Islands, an archipelago of 13 major isles and over 100 rocks and inlets off Ecuador’s coast, have long attracted travelers seeking solitude and wildlife: endemic giant tortoises and marine iguanas, native scalloped hammerhead sharks, and blue-footed boobies, for starters. Nearly 97% of the Galápagos’ land area is a single national park. Visitor access remains tightly managed, making the destination one of the rare places where travelers can experience wildlife on nature’s terms (and, as scientists are learning, occasionally encounter new species, like the deep-sea Microeledone galapagensis, or blue octopus). In 2027 National Geographic–Lindblad Expeditions will celebrate 60 years since Lars-Eric Lindblad introduced travelers to the Galápagos on the first nonscientific civilian expedition voyage, establishing the islands as a premier destination for conservation-minded exploration. The brand doubled its Galápagos fleet in 2025 by adding the 16-guest catamaran Delfina and the 48-guest Gemini. In January 2027 the brand will launch Ultimate Galápagos, a 13-day itinerary aboard the 96-passenger Endeavour II that visits 11 islands including remote Genovesa, known for its red-footed booby colonies. Elsewhere, Natural Habitat Adventures’ Galápagos Tortoise Camp just transitioned to 100% solar power and introduced the Galápagos’ first fully electric panga (a small skiff for excursions)—part of trips booked aboard the brand’s Petrel luxury catamaran—reducing emissions for wildlife excursions and setting a new benchmark for sustainable travel in the destination. —Hannah Selinger Go for: volcano trekking, peak birdwatching, price points that range from shoestring to big spender Long a backpacking destination on the Central America 101 route known as the Gringo Trail, Guatemala is an increasingly popular destination for a generation of young travelers seeking slower, more enriching tourism that won’t break the bank. INGUAT, the Guatemala Institute of Tourism, says that arrival numbers support the TikTok thesis—and are only projected to increase. Some of the appeal is timeless: Guatemalan day-to-day life is deeply steeped in ancient heritage and culture. Sprawling artisan markets like Nim Po’t in Antigua offer easy access to hand-carved and painted wood animal masks, for example, but deeper dives are offered by Antigua-based textile studio Luna Zorro, which organizes craft retreats throughout the country. The brand’s recently opened La Valiente (February 2026) is a two-bedroom guesthouse in the heart of the city, and almost everything at the property—from the bedding to ceramics—is artisan-made by local creators. The country’s natural beauty is also an evergreen draw, but as younger generations embrace the mores—and aesthetics—of hiking (and even birdwatching), trails like the rigorous two-day Acatenango trek are list-toppers in the central highland region that is ripe with some of the 780 species recorded in Guatemala. Many choose to continue to the Tikal National Park in the northeast, where 3,000-year-old ruins of the Maya city sit amid a lush green jungle setting. At the park’s recently reopened Conservation and Research Center, visitors can observe the behind-the-scenes preservation process of ruins and artifacts, only now visible to the public. It all makes for welcome news that Guatemala is getting even easier to access: Frontier is offering daily, seasonal, nonstop service from Los Angeles to Guatemala City from December 17 until January 4, if you need a last-minute holiday getaway, and United Airlines has a permanent direct route from Houston. —Anna Zou Go for: untamed rainforest, immersive eco-lodges, and easier-than-ever access Guyana, South America’s only country with English as its official language, celebrated six decades of nationhood this May. Yet from a small plane bound for Kaieteur Falls, one of the most powerful single-drop waterfalls in the world, the lush rainforest below appears several geological eras older. Perhaps it’s no wonder; an impressive 85% of this country remains forested. Most travelers start in the coastal city of Georgetown, where the country’s Caribbean identity is tangible in the annual Mashramani carnival (every February), vibrant Stabroek Market, and Gothic St. George’s Anglican Cathedral, which is made of wood. But journeys quickly turn toward the rainforest and savanna, with Kaieteur as their most dramatic introduction. At the falls, the Potaro River drops 741 feet from a sandstone ledge—more than four times Niagara’s height—yet just over 8,000 people see it each year, usually on a day flight from Georgetown. A fuller interior journey requires a separate, multiday circuit through Iwokrama International Centre for Rainforest Conservation and Development (IIC), a nearly million-acre reserve managed alongside 20 Indigenous communities, and into the North Rupununi, a landscape of savanna, wetlands, and river villages where Indigenous-led conservation becomes part of the itinerary. For in-the-know travelers, right now—when a host of new expeditions and accommodations have risen to meet vanguard voyage interest—is the time to go. On that circuit, three conservation-linked stays give travelers a direct role in the work. Atta Rainforest Lodge is the base for Iwokrama’s canopy walkway, suspended 100 feet above the forest floor and managed by the reserve in partnership with Makushi communities and local tourism operators. Further into the North Rupununi, road and river lead to Rewa Eco-Lodge, operated by Rewa Village, where anglers help measure and tag arapaima before release. Another tributary leads to Yupukari’s Caiman House, a village-run guesthouse and research station where visitors help researchers study black caiman after dark. The community also raises yellow-spotted Amazon river turtles for release. Reaching these stays still requires small planes and long road-and-river transfers, though one important link is easing: In August 2026, Jags Aviation added a 19-seat turboprop service four days a week between Georgetown’s Eugene F. Correia International Airport and Lethem. Back in Georgetown, the arrival of international hotel brands marks a new era at the start and finish of any trip. The 152-room AC Hotel opened in December 2025, with the 172-room Four Points by Sheraton following in April 2026. A Hilton resort is due on the seafront in 2028. And there are more reasons to linger in 2027: From October 8 to October 17, the capital will also host Carifesta XVI, which will return the Caribbean Festival of Arts to its 1972 birthplace, promising a cultural counterpart to the wilderness of the interior. —Paul Jebara Go for: new off-season expeditions, and a slate of fresh lodges Los Glaciares National Park, with its toothy granite spires, windswept steppe, and glaciers that crack and roar as they calve into milky-blue lakes, has long been the crown jewel of Argentine Patagonia. Yet its main gateway town, El Calafate, hasn’t seen a new luxury hotel in over two decades. That changes in December 2026 with Explora El Calafate, an all-inclusive 20-key lodge snaking across a Patagonian estancia near Lake Argentino. The hotel’s design leans into soothing earth tones—with giant windows framing distant glaciers—while menus highlight Patagonian lamb, trout, and wine. Guides take guests on 30 different adventures out to remote wildlands like the ice fields of Brazo Sur or the bird sanctuary of Laguna Nimez. Explora will simultaneously open a second property just across the Chilean border in its private Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve, further linking the two destinations by building out a binational circuit. Meanwhile, southern Patagonia is shedding its reputation as a summer-only destination. Awasi Patagonia, near Torres del Paine, will now remain open through the 2027 winter season—prime time for puma safaris—while ecotourism operator Chile Nativo extols the virtue of the offseason with its Winter W Trek, tracing the iconic route past Paine Grande and the Grey Glacier in the region’s quieter season. The momentum is even greater in Los Glaciares. In 2026 park concessionaire Hielo & Aventura, responding to greater off-season demand that can help disperse the annual tourist traffic, operated its popular ice hiking excursion atop the Perito Moreno Glacier during the winter for the first time. Unlike most Patagonian mountain towns, El Calafate doesn’t shut down when crowds depart, which means there are still hot chocolates to be had after a day on the ice. —Mark Johanson Go for: a buyout villa in jaguar country, and groundbreaking conservation efforts For flora and fauna lovers headed to South America, the Amazon has long been the marquee trip. But further south, where the waters of the Amazon trickle down into the world’s largest tropical wetland, something different awaits. The Pantanal stretches across 42 million acres in Brazil, Bolivia, and Paraguay. In comparison to the Amazon, it’s a bit more arid, with strong cowboy culture, and the foliage is sparser, making this a great place to spot jaguars in the wild. This is in no small part thanks to important conservation work that has taken place over decades. At the upscale Caiman Pantanal, a trailblazing safari stay in the Brazilian Pantanal, jaguar rescue group Onçafari has an on-site location, allowing guests at the all-inclusive property to explore 131,000 acres of land with the big cat experts who have meticulously tagged and tracked dozens of them. Caiman’s new private villa, Cordilheira, was unveiled in June 2026. It brings together seven bungalows (private infinity pools included) that fit up to 16 people, making it possible for families and groups to have a buyout experience as they spend days tracking jaguars—and tapirs, and giant anteaters, and capybaras—before evenings filled with Brazilian barbecue and folk music under the stars. Operators like Natural Habitat Adventures can continue the journey northbound to destinations like Porto Jofre, where cat sightings happen by boat on the river, and jaguars can be seen chasing caimans at the water’s edge. The conservation work required to protect this rare natural landscape and its fauna is ongoing, but new projects like the Jaguar Rivers Initiative, announced in fall 2025, prove the only way is forward. This new coalition, which connects the aforementioned Onçafari with Kristine Tompkins’s Fundación Rewilding Argentina, Nativa in Bolivia, and Fundación Moisés Bertoni in Paraguay, hopes to better link and restore various jaguar habitats. The goal is, of course, ecological first and foremost—but if the preservation work in Pantanal has taught us anything so far, it’s that great conservation can lead to great wildlife experiences. —Megan Spurrell Go for: uncrowded surf spots, a noteworthy beach hideaway, and plenty of seafood On Peru’s northern coast, life moves slowly in the seaside towns and fishing villages that have long drawn a quiet trickle of visitors including surfers chasing mythical waves, Limeños lured by closer-to-the-equator sun and tranquility, and culinary-minded travelers who know that nowhere else does seafood quite like this part of the country. In the past few years, an increasingly stylish crop of Airbnbs have popped up—like Kahu Beach House in Los Órganos, where modern design uses endemic natural materials and where fantastic surf breaks are visible from your breakfast table. The more recent resort opening of Inkaterra Cabo Blanco in February 2026 has shone an even brighter spotlight: On the same stretch of sand where Marilyn Monroe and Ernest Hemingway vacationed in the 1950s, this contemporary beachside stay with just 13 rooms is an elegant approach to the destination’s barefoot ease, refined coastal dining, and experiences that range from a day on the water with a local fishing collective to surfing and kitesurfing lessons just steps from the private plunge pools. As for the region’s culinary offerings? You won’t have to look hard. This sun-baked stretch of coast is where carne seca dries on clotheslines and makes its way into seco de chavela (a pounded beef and plantain dish bursting with chile), and where Peruvian classics like conchas a la parmesana (scallops baked with cheese) are remixed using conchas negras, a unique shellfish found in the mangroves of Tumbes, near the border with Ecuador. Hearty dishes like picante de mariscos, a seafood stew, sit side by side with chilled raw-fish tiraditos that fly close to the sun in their spice. —Megan Spurrell Go for: kitesurfing for pros—and newbies—in a fishing village now home to quietly luxurious stays Preá has the unmistakable charm of a Brazilian fishing village—a seemingly endless shoreline, a sandy-street village center, and beachfront restaurants serving fresh-caught seafood—with one major difference: wind, and lots of it. From July through early January, this sleepy town catches some of the world’s most consistently powerful gusts, the kind kitesurfers cross oceans for. Now, with the sport growing in popularity, beginners are starting to come too, bringing with them an exciting new energy. Kitesurfing has become so popular among Brazil’s well-heeled travelers that Marco Dalpozzo, a partner at the pioneering pousada Rancho do Peixe, dubbed the sport “the new golf, the new tennis, the new skiing.” Learning takes some commitment: First-timers start on the sand before progressing into the water, with a full beginner course happening over several days. Yet new kitesurfing locations are making it easier than ever for newcomers to join the scene. While the famed Jericoacoara next door is known for its lively nightlife and parties, Preá’s new crop of high-end boutique hotels and villas offers a more exclusive take on barefoot luxury. Think ocean-facing rooms, intimate private villas, and seaside bungalows paired with their own kite schools, full-service spas, and feet-in-the-sand restaurants. Whether you’re up for braving the wind or not, there is plenty else to do in terms of both adventure and restorative wellness. Preá offers easy access to the landscapes that made neighboring Jericoacoara famous. Set off by buggy or quad to explore the region’s enormous sand dunes and freshwater lagoons that naturally occur between them, or visit the otherworldly Jericoacoara National Park. Back in Preá, book a treatment at L’Occitane spa at the Preabeach Boutique Hotel, take advantage of the yoga offerings at Hotel Kabana, or horseback ride along the shore. By sunset, everyone gathers on the beach to watch the last kiters streak across the water as what looks like a giant ball of fire slips into the ocean. Later, dinner can range from candlelit seaside dining to charming restaurants like Casinha in the rustic village center, where flip-flops are acceptable attire. The wind is bringing in major investments too. Grupo Carnaúba is building what it envisions as the wind sports equivalent to an Alpine ski resort. Its members-only Carnaúba Wind House, opened in 2024, offers bungalow stays with a kite center, beach club, restaurant, and freshwater lagoon, while the larger Vila Carnaúba development is adding more luxury residences and beach tennis facilities. The biggest arrival yet comes in 2028, when Anantara opens its first property in the Americas: A beachfront resort complete with its own signature spa and dedicated kitesurfing school. —Carla Vianna Go for: cheffy restaurant openings, a revitalized downtown, and a lineup of literary festivals São Paulo is a city for those with an appetite—for business, culture, and, of course, food. Brazil’s largest and most frenetic metropolis is home to some of Brazil’s most extraordinary architectural landmarks, from Lina Bo Bardi’s museum of art (MASP) to Paulo Mendes da Rocha’s reimagined Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo. Meanwhile, the restaurant landscape has never been more exciting: São Paulo is now home to the only two restaurants in the Southern Hemisphere recently awarded three Michelin stars: Tuju and Evvai. That momentum is reshaping the city well beyond its established dining districts: Near Avenida Paulista, the Mata São Paulo hospitality complex has gathered some of the city’s buzziest names, including Mata Città, Korean barbecue spot Lavva, and pastry chef Antonio Bachour, who opened his first Latin American pastry shop Bachour by Mata here, all in one place. More is on the way, including a new boteco, Á Brasileira, from Janaína Torres (named the World’s Best Female Chef in 2024 by World’s 50 Best). Her beloved Bar da Dona Onça, on the ground floor of Oscar Niemeyer’s sinuous Copan building, has itself gained new neighbors, including seafood-focused Brisa do Barú and Tem Umami!, an ice cream shop with a near-permanent line out the door. Together with an observation deck, the new arrivals are turning the 1,160-apartment Modernist landmark into one of downtown’s liveliest destinations. Also inside the Copan is Livraria Megafauna, part of a new wave of independent bookstores bringing literary life back to São Paulo’s streets. Its Poesia no Centro poetry festival, returning in April 2027, has already become a fixture on the city’s cultural calendar; meanwhile the growing Feira do Livro, organized by literary magazine Quatro Cinco Um, is expected to draw around 100,000 people to the Praça Charles Miller in May 2027, and it will nearly double the space devoted to its mostly independent publishers. That literary boom is part of a broader cultural surge, with major events like SP-Arte in April and the Bienal de São Paulo—Latin America’s largest visual arts event—returning to Ibirapuera Park in September. The expansion of Museu de Arte de São Paulo Assis Chateaubriand, the city’s landmark art museum, only adds to the momentum: Its newest building, opened in March 2025, increased exhibition space by more than 60% and made room for new shows and works from the collection previously kept out of public view. —Rafael Tonon
